title: Digital corporate responsibility as an element of corporate social responsibility (a case study of Ukrainian agricultural enterprises)
summary: The article aims to substantiate the theoretical, methodological, and practical foundations of Digital Corporate Responsibility (DCR/CDR) as a direction of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) amid the comprehensive digitalization of business processes, focusing on Ukraine’s agricultural sector. The study applies dialectical analysis and synthesis, grouping, structural-functional analysis, and case study methods. The results show that digitalization creates significant opportunities to improve the efficiency, productivity, and profitability of agribusiness while generating new ethical, social, and environmental risks, including cybersecurity threats, algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, the carbon footprint of IT infrastructure, and electronic waste. DCR is therefore considered an important mechanism for mitigating these risks and ensuring socially and environmentally responsible digital transformation. The scientific novelty lies in substantiating DCR within three interrelated ESG dimensions: digital environmental (E), digital social (S), and digital governance (G) responsibility. The study shows that implementing DCR can strengthen stakeholder relations, transparency, trust, and the sustainable development potential of agricultural companies. The experience of leading Ukrainian agricultural holdings, including Astarta and Kernel, illustrates practical approaches to combining digital technologies with responsible business practices. The research’s practical significance lies in the proposed use of corporate digital ethics codes to strengthen cybersecurity, protect digital rights, develop digital culture, and promote responsible digital behavior among employees and stakeholders. Further research should focus on developing a comprehensive system of indicators to assess the level of DCR, identifying relevant ESG criteria, and adapting international approaches and best practices to the institutional and socio-economic conditions of Ukrainian agribusiness. Keywords: Digital Corporate Responsibility, Corporate Social Responsibility, digitalization, digital transformation, ESG, agricultural sector, agribusiness, precision agriculture, digital ethics, sustainable development, cybersecurity, stakeholders.

title: FROM CSR TO ESG: EVOLUTION OF CORPORATE RESPONSIBILITY AND ITS IMPACT ON BUSINESS PERFORMANCE
summary: Corporate responsibility has undergone a significant transformation from traditional philanthropyand voluntary social initiatives to an integrated framework of Environmental, Social and Governance(ESG) performance. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) established the principle that companieshave responsibilities beyond profit generation, while ESG has developed a more structured languagefor measuring environmental impacts, social relationships, governance quality and sustainability-related risks. This article examines the evolution from CSR to ESG and analyses its implications forbusiness performance. Recent empirical evidence from India indicates that ESG disclosure can bepositively associated with firm performance, although findings differ according to industry,measurement methodology, time period and the specific performance indicator used. The articleargues that the business value of ESG is strongest when responsibility is embedded into strategy, riskmanagement, operations and governance rather than treated merely as a reporting exercise.

title: A provincial environmental technology transition indicator for Vietnam: Green finance, spatial diffusion, and absorptive capacity
summary: This paper develops and validates a provincial Environmental Technology Transition (ETT) indicator for Vietnam and uses it to assess whether green finance is associated with cleaner technology upgrading, eco-innovation, and energy-efficiency improvement. Using a balanced panel of 63 Vietnamese provinces over 2014-2024 (693 observations), the study combines indicator construction, principal-component validation, Spatial Durbin modelling, and an IV-spatial estimator to examine both within-province and cross-province technology-transition dynamics. The preferred S2SLS-SDM estimate indicates that a one-standard-deviation increase in green finance intensity is associated with a 0.334 standard-deviation increase in the ETT indicator (p<0.01). The spatial multiplier (M = 1.30) indicates amplification under coordinated regional shocks relative to an isolated provincial response, while the full green-finance impact also depends on the estimated direct and spatially lagged coefficients (Section 5.2). Institutional quality approximately doubles the marginal return to green finance, indicating that absorptive capacity and implementation quality condition the effectiveness of green-finance instruments. The findings support a sequencing strategy in which green-credit expansion, innovation capacity, and institutional strengthening are treated as complementary elements of environmental technology transition policy.

title: Mechanisms for ensuring the digital transformation of industrial enterprises
summary: The article examines the aspects of the digital transformation of industrial enterprises amid technological, economic, and institutional change. The study is relevant because digital transformation has moved beyond implementing individual information systems and technological solutions to encompass changes in business processes, organizational approaches, management systems, resource utilization, and mechanisms for creating economic value. For Ukrainian industrial enterprises, this issue has become particularly urgent because they must simultaneously restore production capacity, modernize technology, maintain operational resilience, and adapt to the new requirements of the digital economy. The study aims to analyze and systematize the theoretical and methodological framework for developing mechanisms for industrial enterprises’ digital transformation. To achieve this purpose, the article clarifies the concepts of “digitization,” “digitalization,” and “digital transformation.” It establishes that the digital transformation of an industrial enterprise should be viewed as a systemic process of restructuring technological, production, managerial, organizational, and market relationships through the integration of digital technologies, data, and digital competencies. Unlike fragmented automation of individual operations, digital transformation involves extending technological changes across interconnected business processes, the management system, and value-creation mechanisms. The conditions for digital transformation in industrial enterprises fall into four main groups: technological, organizational, resource-related, and institutional. Technological conditions include digital infrastructure, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, robotics, big data, and digital twins; organizational and intangible conditions include digital culture, competencies, organizational flexibility, strategic orientation, managerial support, and data governance; resource-related conditions include financial, investment, human, information, and time resources; institutional conditions include public policy, financial support, the regulatory environment, the innovation ecosystem, and international integration. This study examines current trends in digital development in enterprises in the European Union and Ukraine and identifies differences in the adoption of basic and advanced digital technologies. For Ukrainian industrial enterprises, insufficient financial and human capacity to scale digital solutions remains a significant constraint, particularly amid wartime uncertainty and competition for resources between restoring production capacities and investing in digital solutions. The mechanism for ensuring digital transformation should be an integrated system of interconnected technological, organizational, financial, human-resource, informational, and institutional components. Align the digital strategy with the enterprise’s overall development strategy, secure adequate resources and financial support, develop employees’ digital competencies, integrate digital technologies into key business processes, and account for digital maturity, financial capacity, production-specific characteristics, and external environmental risks. Keywords: digital transformation, digitalization, industrial enterprises, financial support, digital investments, financial mechanisms, digital maturity.

title: Digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing: the mediating role of supply chain complexity in technology-driven operations
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing firms, with particular attention to the statistical mediating role of supply chain complexity. It addresses the limited understanding of how digital technologies, including AI, IoT, and cybersecurity, operate collectively rather than in isolation. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capability view (DCV), the study employs a quantitative research design using survey data from 732 managerial and supervisory respondents working in manufacturing firms in Mississippi, West Virginia, and Arkansas. Structural equation modeling (SEM) using AMOS is applied to test the proposed relationships. Findings The results indicate that digital ecosystems are positively associated with supply chain resilience, with cybersecurity exhibiting the strongest association with the Digital Ecosystem construct. Supply chain complexity shows a positive but comparatively smaller association with resilience and the statistically significant indirect relationship is consistent with partial mediation. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to manufacturing firms in selected U.S. states, which may affect generalizability. Future research could explore cross-industry and cross-country contexts and examine additional mediating or moderating mechanisms. Practical implications The findings suggest that managers should consider investing in integrated digital infrastructure, prioritizing cybersecurity capabilities and using data-driven technologies while proactively managing the complexity of digital transformation. Originality/value This study advances a systems-level understanding of digital ecosystems in supply chains by showing that integrated digital capabilities, rather than isolated technologies, are positively associated with resilience in complex operational environments.

title: Review Protocol — Intellectual Capital and Market Performance: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: This document is the protocol for a systematic literature review of the relationship between intellectual capital (IC) and market-based firm performance. It was deposited before the final literature search to fix the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy, and analysis plan in advance. The review addresses four research questions: (1) the development and structure of research on IC and market performance; (2) the theories, methods, IC and market performance proxies, and contexts used; (3) why empirical findings diverge across IC components and proxies, market performance measures, countries, sectors, and methods; and (4) the extent to which ESG, earnings quality, and corporate governance have been examined as mediators or moderators. Scopus is the main database, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation chasing. Eligible studies are English-language journal articles up to 2025 that use archival firm-level data and test IC as an independent variable against at least one market-based performance measure (e.g., Tobin's Q, market-to-book ratio, stock return). The review combines bibliometric analysis (VOSviewer) with content synthesis, tests five competing explanations for divergent findings, and reports gaps as counts; a meta-analysis of partial correlations is planned if data allow. Reporting follows PRISMA 2020. AI tools (Elicit, NotebookLM) assist screening and are verified by the author.

title: Audit Committee Size and Financial Reporting Quality of Listed Non-Financial Firms in Nigeria
summary: Main purpose: This study examined the effect of audit committee size on the financial reporting quality of non-financial firms listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX). Methodology: Secondary data were obtained from the annual reports of 58 sampled non-financial firms, drawn from a population of 106 listed firms, covering the period from 2013 to 2024. The data were analysed using panel regression estimation techniques to determine the effect of audit committee size and relevant firm-specific variables on financial reporting quality. Findings: The results revealed that audit committee size had a positive and statistically significant effect on financial reporting quality (t = 2.2511, p < 0.05), indicating that larger audit committees may provide broader oversight of the financial reporting process. Leverage also had a positive and statistically significant effect on financial reporting quality (t = 2.0864, p < 0.05). In contrast, audit firm size had a negative and statistically significant association with financial reporting quality (t = −3.1325, p < 0.05), suggesting that the use of larger audit firms does not necessarily translate into higher financial reporting quality among the sampled firms. Practical implications: Boards of listed non-financial firms should maintain appropriately constituted audit committees with sufficient membership and members possessing relevant financial and accounting expertise to strengthen oversight of the financial reporting process. Corporate boards and regulators should also pay closer attention to audit committee composition, leverage practices and the effectiveness of external audit arrangements rather than relying solely on audit firm size as an indicator of reporting quality. Originality/novelty: This study extends the Nigerian corporate governance literature by applying Shivakumar’s (2003) accounting-quality model to examine the effect of audit committee size on financial reporting quality among listed non-financial firms, thereby providing context-specific evidence from a segment characterised by distinct regulatory and governance frameworks. title: Supply Chain Resilience Optimization Integrating Transformers and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: INTRODUCTION: Manufacturing supply chains face increasing vulnerabilities from delayed risk identification, conflicting node-level decisions, and escalating recovery costs, particularly under complex disruption scenarios. Existing approaches often lack proactive, coordinated responses across autonomous supply chain nodes, limiting their ability to anticipate disruptions and synchronize mitigation actions effectively. To address these gaps, this paper proposes an integrated resilience optimization framework that combines predictive analytics with multi-agent coordination. OBJECTIVES: The primary objective is to develop a supply chain resilience framework, termed T-MARL, that enables autonomous suppliers, manufacturers, warehousing nodes, and distributors to: (1) predict future disruption probabilities using temporal risk precursor data, and (2) execute coordinated, proactive replenishment, production, and distribution decisions under inventory and capacity constraints. The framework aims to improve resilience index, reduce total operating costs, and shorten recovery time compared to baseline strategies, while also examining the sensitivity of performance gains to prediction noise and communication latency. METHODS: The T-MARL framework models each supply chain node as an independent agent. A lightweight Transformer captures temporal features from 6-dimensional risk precursor sequences over 12 consecutive periods to forecast disruption probabilities. These predictions feed into a value-decomposition multi-agent reinforcement learning mechanism with centralized training–decentralized execution, where a value-decomposition network orchestrates cross-node actions. Risk-constrained action gating ensures that proactive responses adhere to inventory and capacity limits. A digital twin simulation environment was built with fixed random seeds, covering three scenarios—single-source supply disruption, demand surge, and compound disruption. Five strategies were tested, with 30 runs per unit using common random number pairing. RESULTS: On the trajectory-held-out test set, the Transformer achieved an AUC of 0.722 and an F1-score of 0.586, while Random Forest achieved a slightly higher AUC of 0.724. Under the compound disruption scenario, T-MARL attained a resilience index of 0.849—a 1.63 percentage-point gain over VDN-MARL -reduced total cost by 14.7%, and shortened average recovery time from 1.67 periods to zero. T-MARL also achieved lower operating costs while maintaining service levels comparable to rule-based strategies. However, the paper also found that prediction noise and communication latency diminish these performance gains. CONCLUSION: This research contributes a reproducible digital twin analysis framework for disruption prediction, cross-node collaborative response, and rapid recovery in manufacturing supply chains. While T-MARL demonstrates significant improvements in resilience and cost-efficiency under ideal conditions, practical deployment must account for real-world imperfections such as noisy forecasts and delayed communications. The framework provides a scalable foundation for future work on adaptive, data-driven supply chain resilience.

title: Tax Evasion, Corporate Governance, and ESG Disclosure: A Systematic Literature Review of Emerging Patterns and Research Frontiers (2000–2025)
summary: This study presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of 95 peer-reviewed international and national journal articles published between 2020 and 2025, examining the interrelationships among tax morale, agency problems, institutional quality, sustainability pressure, and ESG disclosure in the context of corporate tax evasion and avoidance. Following the PRISMA protocol, this review synthesizes evidence drawn from leading databases including Scopus, ScienceDirect, Emerald Insight, and Taylor & Francis Online, as well as top-ranked Indonesian journals indexed in Sinta 1 and Sinta 2. The findings consistently demonstrate that elevated tax morale, anchored in ethical consciousness and robust social norms, substantially curtails opportunistic tax behavior and strengthens compliance among both individual taxpayers and corporate entities. Nonetheless, agency conflicts remain a structural challenge: information asymmetries between managers and stakeholders frequently precipitate reduced transparency, earnings manipulation, and aggressive tax avoidance strategies—particularly in institutional environments characterized by weak regulatory enforcement. Conversely, high-quality institutional frameworks—marked by sound governance mechanisms, credible regulatory bodies, and effective rule of law significantly mitigate agency costs and enhance the reliability of ESG disclosures. The review also reveals a growing convergence between sustainability mandates and tax governance: as regulators, investors, and civil society intensify pressure for responsible corporate behavior, firms increasingly improve the scope and credibility of their ESG reporting, which in turn constrains tax aggressiveness. This review contributes to the literature by mapping the theoretical evolution of tax research, identifying persistent methodological gaps, and proposing an integrative agenda that aligns tax policy, corporate governance, and sustainable development. Implications for policymakers and practitioners especially in developing economies such as Indonesia are discussed in detail. Keywords: Agency Problem; Corporate Governance; ESG Disclosure; Institutional Quality; Systematic Literature Review; Tax Evasion; Tax Morale.

title: An integrated scientometric and BERTopic-based analysis on examining the role of artificial intelligence in achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
summary: This study investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through a comprehensive scientometric analysis. It explores the evolution of scholarly research, identifies leading contributors, maps thematic trends, examines how AI technologies contribute to advancing sustainability across multiple domains, and identifies latent semantic themes. A total of 3262 unique scholarly records published between 1989 and 2025, after deduplication and screening, were finalized from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The dataset was analysed using Biblioshiny (R-based Bibliometrix) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, citation impact, collaborative networks, thematic evolution, and conceptual structures. Indicators such as Relative Growth Rate (RGR), Doubling Time (DT), h-index, g-index, and Lotka’s Law were applied to evaluate research productivity and scholarly influence. In addition, BERTopic-based abstract-level topic modelling was applied to identify latent semantic themes, SDG-linked thematic domains, temporal evolution and potential research gaps. Results reveal a significant growth in AI-SDG research, particularly after 2015, with an accelerated increase post-2020. India, USA, and China emerged as the most productive contributors, while countries like USA, India, United Kingdom and Australia lead in research impact and citation quality. Thematic evolution analysis reveals a transition from foundational themes such as AI, machine learning, climate change, and decision support systems toward more integrated and sustainability-oriented research themes, including sustainable development and SDGs. Thematic linkages further demonstrate the persistent foundational role of AI and machine learning, alongside the growing centrality of climate change and sustainable development, reflecting the increasing convergence of AI research with global sustainability priorities. BERTopic analysis further revealed eleven interpretable abstract-level thematic domains after excluding one heterogeneous outlier category. The dominant themes included digital transformation and green innovation, AI-enabled education, digital health, smart agriculture, renewable energy systems, clean water and sanitation, remote sensing, NLP-based decision support, sustainable construction, tourism, and sustainable chemistry/pharmaceutical applications. This study maps the AI–SDG research landscape by integrating bibliometric indicators with thematic evolution, conceptual analysis, and abstract-level semantic topic modelling. The findings provide insights into the development and thematic orientation of AI-related research in the context of sustainable development. The use of BERTopic complements conventional bibliometric approaches by examining semantic patterns within publication abstracts alongside keyword and citation-based analyses.

title: CORPORATE GOVERNANCE, GENDER DIVERSITY, DAN ESG DISCLOSURE: IMPLIKASI TERHADAP KINERJA PERUSAHAAN DAN KEBERLANJUTAN
summary: Corporate governance and gender diversity have become strategic factors in enhancing the effectiveness of ESG disclosure and integrated reporting (IR). This article presents a narrative literature review of 18 selected scientific articles published between 2019 and 2025, analyzed through a process of identification, screening, and relevance evaluation based on the research topics of corporate governance, gender diversity, and ESG disclosure. The reviewed literature examines the relationship between corporate governance practices, gender diversity on boards of directors and senior management, and the quality of ESG disclosure. The findings indicate that strong governance mechanisms and adequate gender diversity are positively associated with improved ESG disclosure quality and firm performance. Comprehensive ESG disclosure contributes to reducing the cost of capital, increasing firm value, and strengthening corporate reputation, particularly in the context of emerging markets. This article identifies research gaps related to the influence of local institutions, cultural contexts, and the adoption of digital technologies in supporting ESG disclosure, while providing practical implications for regulators and companies in strengthening sustainable business practices. ABSTRAK Corporate governance dan gender diversity menjadi faktor strategis dalam meningkatkan efektivitas ESG disclosure dan integrated reporting (IR). Artikel ini menyajikan tinjauan naratif terhadap 18 artikel ilmiah terpilih periode 2019–2025 yang dianalisis melalui proses identifikasi, screening, dan evaluasi relevansi berdasarkan topik corporate governance, gender diversity, dan ESG disclosure.yang mengkaji hubungan antara praktik tata kelola perusahaan, keberagaman gender pada dewan direksi dan manajemen, serta kualitas ESG disclosure. title: Provincial Carbon Inequality and the Effectiveness of Green Finance Development in China
summary: ABSTRACT Development disparities within regions cause carbon inequality (CI), which exacerbates the Chinese unbalanced development problem. However, there is still a lack of research that measures CI from the aspect of intra‐regional differences and examines its impact factors. Using sub‐provincial data covering 420 cities, counties, and districts, this study measures CI in 30 Chinese provinces and investigates the influence of green finance (GF) on CI and the role of climate risk (CR) in the GF‐CI linkage. Several findings have been found. First, using the population‐weighted Williamson index to capture intra‐provincial disparities, our analysis reveals pronounced regional variation in CI, with the East and Middle regions following a U‐shaped pattern between 2008 and 2017, while the West experiences a consistent decline. Second, the dynamic panel analysis reveals that GF can reduce CI, particularly in midwestern regions and provinces characterised by lower carbon intensity. Third, the moderating effect demonstrates that climate risk (CR) weakens the inhibitory role of GF on CI. Under low CR, GF mitigates CI, whereas when CR exceeds a critical threshold, the beneficial effect of GF is reversed. This study contributes empirical insights for policymakers seeking to mitigate CI through financial instruments.

title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN EARNINGS MANAGEMENT AND AUDIT QUALITY: A CASE STUDY OF NESTLÉ NIGERIA PLC
summary: This study examined the relationship between audit quality and earnings management in Nestlé Nigeria Plc and assessed how audit quality contributes to the credibility and reliability of financial reporting. A descriptive and explanatory design was used, with data obtained from 40 purposively selected respondents comprising finance/accounting staff, internal and external auditors, and investors/shareholders. Questionnaire responses were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation and regression techniques. The findings showed positive perceptions of audit quality: competence/expertise recorded a mean of 4.35, compliance with standards 4.40, and high-quality audits enhancing financial-statement reliability 4.45. The regression analysis showed that audit quality had a significant negative effect on earnings management (β = −0.475, t = −6.10, p < .01), while corporate governance also had a significant negative effect (β = −0.285, t = −3.95, p = .001). The model explained 61% of the variation in earnings management (R² = .61; F = 22.75; p < .01). The study concludes that stronger audit quality is associated with lower earnings management and greater confidence in financial reporting. It recommends continued emphasis on auditor independence, professional skepticism, internal controls, and effective audit-committee oversight.

title: Business Continuity and Climate Change: Firms’ Risk Perceptions and Adaptive Measures
summary: Climate change-related hazards are increasingly affecting the physical assets, production processes, and supply chains of industrial enterprises. This study aims to evaluate the impacts of climate change-related hazards on business continuity in firms operating within OIZs as part of the RESMAR Project. As part of the research, a survey was conducted among firms operating in nine OIZs located in the Marmara Region, and the data obtained were analysed. The findings indicate that there are no statistically significant sectoral differences in firms' levels of exposure to climate change-related hazards. Instead, firms' geographical location, the infrastructure capacity of the OIZs in which they operate, and their dependence on supply chains emerged as the primary determinants of climate-related impacts. Firms operating in labour-intensive industries, such as the textile sector, and those in high-technology industries, such as the defence sector, were found to exhibit greater sensitivity to climate change. These findings highlight the need for climate change adaptation strategies in industrial enterprises to extend beyond facility-level risk management and incorporate measures aimed at strengthening supply chain resilience and enhancing the climate resilience of OIZ infrastructure.

title: Digital transformation as a driver of participation in global value chains
summary: The article examines how digital transformation deepens countries’ participation in global value chains. The study aims to substantiate the mechanisms through which digitalization influences countries’ integration into global production networks and to identify strategic directions for strengthening trade and digital development. The study uses systems analysis, comparison, generalization, and synthesis of international experience. The findings show that digital technologies reduce transaction costs, improve coordination efficiency, and facilitate cross-border trade procedures. The results indicate that digital infrastructure alone is insufficient to ensure deeper participation in GVCs, as its effects depend on complementarity with trade openness, trade facilitation, and investment linkages. Broadband and mobile infrastructure create the basis for digital inclusion, while trade openness strengthens integration into international production networks. At the same time, FDI does not automatically generate technology and knowledge spillovers, highlighting the importance of linkages between foreign investors and local SMEs. International experience demonstrates that Smart Customs and Single Window systems can reduce administrative and time costs in cross-border trade. Integrating these systems with artificial intelligence, distributed ledger technologies, and the Internet of Things expands opportunities for digital verification, customs control, cargo monitoring, and supply-chain transparency. These mechanisms can facilitate SME integration into GVCs by reducing barriers to international production networks. The study’s scientific novelty lies in developing an integrated approach that combines digital, trade, and investment mechanisms for GVC integration. The study’s practical significance is reflected in the proposed strategic directions for trade and digital policy. Further research should quantitatively assess the complementary effects of digital readiness and trade facilitation on countries’ participation in GVCs. title: Mission command and supply chain resilience in wartime military logistics: empirical evidence from the Ukrainian Armed Forces
summary: Purpose This study investigates how command, control and leadership mechanisms enable supply chain resilience (SCRES) in wartime military logistics, addressing a gap in empirical research on organizational and command factors under adversarial conditions. Design/methodology/approach We collected survey data (n = 82) from logistics experts in the Ukrainian Armed Forces (UAF) and analyzed the structural relationships among mission command (MC), leader–member exchange (LMX), planning (PLAN), visibility (VIS), responsiveness (RESP) and recovery (REC) using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) combined with necessary condition analysis (NCA). Findings The structural model yielded predictive relevance (R2 RESP = 0.705, R2 REC = 0.415). RESP emerged as the strongest predictor of REC (β = 0.542), the central mediating pathway to resilience outcomes. MC strongly predicted RESP (β = 0.477), indirectly influencing REC through this pathway. MC and RESP showed close empirical overlap, plausibly reflecting MC's doctrinal role in producing responsiveness, though this warrants cautious interpretation. LMX strengthened resilience indirectly by supporting MC. NCA revealed that VIS and MC function as necessary conditions for achieving high REC, even when their direct effects are nonsignificant in SEM. Originality/value By integrating PLS-SEM with NCA, we offer a leadership-centered explanation of SCRES in wartime military operations. The findings are consistent with perceptual evidence of NATO-aligned MC practices among surveyed UAF logistics personnel, underscoring their role in sustaining supply chain resilience. These insights primarily inform military logistics, with potential relevance for how command-and-control affects resilience in other high-stakes environments.

title: Unplanned Urbanisation and the Right to a Healthy Environment: Rethinking Environmental Governance in Himachal Pradesh
summary: Abstract Himachal Pradesh presents an unusually demanding setting for environmental governance because urban growth takes place on steep, geologically fragile and disaster-prone terrain while being driven by tourism, transport infrastructure, housing demand and expanding commercial activity. The resulting legal problem is not simply whether individual projects comply with environmental statutes, but whether the cumulative pattern of urbanisation is compatible with the constitutional obligation to secure a healthy environment. This article examines the relationship between unplanned urbanisation and the right to a healthy environment in Himachal Pradesh, with particular attention to Shimla and the wider Himalayan urban context. It argues that Indian environmental law has already developed the constitutional and doctrinal foundations necessary for an integrated model of ecological urban governance, but those foundations remain institutionally fragmented. Town planning, municipal regulation, environmental clearance, forest protection, disaster management, waste regulation and climate adaptation are commonly administered through separate legal channels even though they operate on the same ecological system. The article analyses Article 21, Articles 47, 48A and 51A(g), the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, the Himachal Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act 1977, municipal legislation, the Environmental Impact Assessment framework and the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court and National Green Tribunal. It particularly examines the Supreme Court's decisions in State of Himachal Pradesh v Yogendera Mohan Sengupta (2024) and M/s Pristine Hotels and Resorts Pvt Ltd v State of Himachal Pradesh (2025), alongside the continuing judicial scrutiny of Himachal's ecological condition. The article proposes a framework of ecological urban governance based on carrying capacity, risk-sensitive zoning, cumulative impact assessment, climate-resilient planning, transparent environmental data, meaningful public participation and enforceable development controls. It concludes that the right to a healthy environment should operate not merely as a remedial right after pollution or disaster occurs, but as a substantive planning principle governing where, how and at what intensity urban development may lawfully occur in a fragile Himalayan state.

title: Assessing the Influence of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) Adoption on Financial Transparency and Investor Confidence
summary: This systematic literature review synthesizes evidence on the association between International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) adoption and two outcome domains: financial transparency and financial reporting quality, and investor confidence and capital-market outcomes. The review draws on 41 empirical, conceptual, and review-based studies across multiple institutional and geopolitical contexts. The assessment focuses on empirical evidence indicating that IFRS implementation is frequently associated with improvements in financial reporting quality, especially in terms of comparability and transparency. The reviewed literature also suggests that these reporting improvements may support investor confidence and capital-market development, although the magnitude and consistency of these associations vary across institutional settings. Evidence further indicates that IFRS-related benefits are conditional on regulatory enforcement, institutional quality, corporate governance, organizational readiness, and regional stability. Barriers such as limited professional capacity, technical complexity, training costs, and geopolitical uncertainty can restrict reform effectiveness, particularly in developing and conflict-affected economies. The review contributes by integrating reporting and investor-facing outcomes, highlighting boundary conditions that explain divergent findings, and identifying future research gaps related to non-financial metrics, ESG reporting, longitudinal effects, and IFRS adoption in unstable institutional contexts. The paper concludes that IFRS adoption can support global financial harmonization, but its benefits depend on complementary institutions, effective enforcement, and local contextual fit.

title: Determinants of Key Audit Matters (KAMs) Disclosure: Empirical Evidence from an Emerging Economy
summary: The introduction of new audit requirements regarding the disclosure of KAMs enhances the communicational value of audit reports. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to examine the impact of auditors’ characteristics and corporate governance characteristics on key audit matters (KAMs) disclosure in auditors’ report in an emerging economy like Bangladesh. Herein, DS30 companies listed in DSE from 2018 to 2023 are taken as a sample because it starts after the mandatory implementation of ISA 701 and KAM reporting requirements in Bangladesh and provides enough time to observe meaningful changes in KAM disclosure practices. Using a multivariate pooled OLS regression analysis, this study finds significant positive association of auditors’ attributes (BIG4, FEMA, AFEE and ATENURE) on disclosure of KAMs. Additionally, among the corporate governance characteristics BIND and ACIND have significant positive impacts on the disclosure of KAMs whereas ACEXP has significant negative effect on the disclosure of KAMs. This study additionally reinforces the significance of women’s involvement in the growth of emerging economies and emphasizes the value of women’s engagement and ongoing professional development. Thus, the findings of the study contribute to Agency Theory, Resource Dependence Theory and Upper Echelons Theory by showing how auditor and governance characteristics influence KAM disclosure through monitoring, resource, and judgement-based mechanisms. The study’s findings also assist standard-setters, regulators, and those who produce financial statements by giving them a better knowledge of the factors that could influence a decision to report KAMs by an auditor. However, new areas for future research could include the perception of new regulations by auditors, the strength of auditors’ resources, the presence of women in senior management, the interaction between female auditors and female audit committee members, as well as family ownership.

title: The Church as a Feeding Community in Acts 2:42-47 And its Implications for Corporate Social Responsibility in the Redeemed Christian Church of God, Ogun State, Nigeria
summary: Abstract The duty of the Church extends beyond spiritual teachings such as personal transformation, financial upliftment, moral growth and human behaviour. The New Testament emphasizes the Church’s role in responding to people’s needs, as depicted in Acts 2:42-47. However, the Church’s response to these social issues has been the subject of debate among scholars. Hence, this study examined the role of the Church as a feeding community in Acts 2:42-47 and its implications for corporate social responsibility (CSR) in the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), Ogun State. The study employed a mixed-methods approach that included a descriptive survey and a historical-critical hermeneutical approach. While the survey used a questionnaire to gather information from respondents, content analysis was used to analyze the biblical text under study. The study population comprised all members of the RCCG in two LGAs of Ogun State. 300 respondents were selected using a stratified sampling technique. Secondary data were drawn from Acts 2:42-47, and the study employed a self-administered, unstructured questionnaire for primary data collection. Findings revealed that although the RCCG has demonstrated acts of kindness by engaging in various CSR initiatives to address poverty, food insecurity, lack of education, among others, these initiatives have not addressed the aforementioned social challenges. Thus, the study recommended, among others, that the RCCG should prioritize personal growth over the distribution of unsustainable material aid. Also, the church should establish microfinance banks across Nigeria that can facilitate loans at low interest rates. Keywords: Acts 2:42-47, corporate social responsibility, feeding community, RCCG

title: FinTech innovation, financial ecological environment, and industry-finance integration: evidence from chinese firms
summary: Industry-finance integration serves as an essential pathway for financial services to support the real economy. This study examines its effect on firms’ total factor productivity. The results indicate that industry-finance integration enhances firms’ TFP by alleviating financing constraints, improving corporate profitability, and strengthening firms’ risk-taking capacity. Moreover, this positive effect is further amplified in regions characterized by higher levels of FinTech advancement and more robust financial ecological environment. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the TFP gains associated with industry-finance integration are especially evident among state-owned enterprises, large firms, and companies led by managers with financial expertise. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of how external environments shape the outcomes of industry-finance integration and offers valuable insights for promoting its sound development to better serve the real economy.

title: Does Digital Transformation Drive the Adjustment of Bank Loan Structure? Evidence From China
summary: ABSTRACT This article examines the impact of digital transformation on bank loan structure. We employ text mining and the entropy weight method to measure the five‐dimensional digital transformation index of banks and conduct an empirical analysis based on the panel data of 132 commercial banks in China from 2013 to 2022. The results indicate that digital transformation significantly drives the adjustment of various types of bank loan structures, increasing the proportion of unsecured loans, personal loans, medium‐ and long‐term loans, manufacturing loans, and green loans. In terms of the impact mechanism, improving information screening capability and enhancing risk control capability are two key channels through which digital transformation exerts its impact. Furthermore, the heterogeneity analysis reveals that the impact of digital transformation on loan structures varies among banks with different asset size, profitability, and management efficiency. Finally, we propose targeted suggestions for commercial banks and regulatory authorities.

title: Lifelong Learning in the Context of Digital Transformation: The Changing Role of Universities
summary: Digital transformation is reshaping the conditions under which universities organize education, recognize learning, and engage with society. Although higher education has traditionally focused on degree programmes undertaken during early adulthood, contemporary technological and social changes require educational opportunities across the life course. This conceptual article examines the relationship between digital transformation, lifelong learning, and the changing role of universities. Drawing on selected scholarly publications and international policy documents, it argues that meaningful transformation requires more than the adoption of digital platforms. Universities need coordinated institutional arrangements that support flexible participation, recognition of prior learning, inclusive pedagogy, ethical technological practices, and sustained community engagement. The article proposes a framework comprising five interconnected dimensions: access, support, recognition, governance, and public value. It also examines tensions between employability and broader educational purposes, flexibility and credential fragmentation, and technological personalization and learner autonomy. The central argument is that universities should approach lifelong learning as an institution-wide educational responsibility. Digital transformation should consequently be evaluated through learning quality, equitable participation, and social contribution, alongside operational efficiency. The article concludes with recommendations for institutional development and directions for empirical research.

title: GLOBAL CLIMATE GOVERNANCE AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES: THE ROLE OF THE UNITED NATIONS IN FACILITATING COOPERATION
summary: Climate change had emerged as a global governance challenge that required coordinated responses among states and international organizations. This study examined the role and effectiveness of international organizations in addressing climate change, with emphasis on climate financing, policy coordination, technical assistance, capacity building, mitigation, adaptation and international cooperation. The study adopted a descriptive research design and relied on secondary data obtained through documentary review. Data were drawn from peer-reviewed journal articles, scholarly books, international agreements, policy documents, institutional reports, climate assessments and publications on climate governance. Purposively selected documents were analyzed using thematic and qualitative content analysis, with evidence coded, categorized and synthesized according to the research questions. Institutional theory was adopted as theoretical framework.The findings revealed that international organizations had made contributions to climate action through the mobilization and allocation of climate finance, coordination of climate policies and commitments, provision of technical assistance, capacity building, mitigation and adaptation support, technology and knowledge cooperation, and facilitation of climate negotiations. However, their contributions had been constrained by institutional fragmentation, inadequate and difficult-to-access climate finance, divergent national interests, weak administrative and technical capacity, poor inter-institutional coordination, gaps between international commitments and domestic implementation, technology and knowledge deficits, and the economic and institutional vulnerabilities of developing countries, particularly African states. The study further found that international climate programmes and agreements did not necessarily constitute effectiveness; rather, effectiveness was reflected in measurable mitigation, adaptation, resilience and implementation outcomes. Accountability, transparency, monitoring and reporting were also identified as essential for assessing progress and strengthening implementation. The study concluded that international organizations had remained central to climate governance, but their effectiveness had depended on translating international commitments, financial resources, technical knowledge and institutional mechanisms into sustained climate action. The study recommended stronger institutional coordination, improved accessibility and targeting of climate finance, sustained capacity building, appropriate technology and knowledge transfer, and stronger accountability and monitoring mechanisms, particularly in developing countries and Africa.

title: THE UNITED NATIONS AND THE EVOLUTION OF GLOBAL CLIMATE GOVERNANCE: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE EMERGING CHALLENGES FACING THE UNFCCC, KYOTO PROTOCOL AND PARIS AGREEMENT, 1992–2025
summary: The study examined the evolution of global climate governance under the United Nations, with particular attention to the emerging challenges confronting the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement between 1992 and 2025. The study was motivated by the persistent gap between the development of increasingly sophisticated international climate institutions and the limited progress in translating international commitments into sufficiently effective, coordinated and equitable climate action. The study adopted a qualitative documentary research design and relied on secondary data obtained from the UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, Conference of the Parties decisions, climate finance documents, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports, United Nations publications and relevant peer-reviewed scholarly literature. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis, guided by Institutional Theory and the institutional effectiveness perspective. The findings revealed that United Nations climate governance had undergone substantial institutional evolution from the framework-based approach of the UNFCCC to the differentiated legally binding commitments of the Kyoto Protocol and subsequently to the universal, nationally determined and transparency-oriented architecture of the Paris Agreement. The study further found that this institutional evolution reflected processes of institutional learning and adaptation, but had not produced commensurate environmental outcomes. Seven major challenges were identified: implementation gaps, inadequate and difficult-to-access climate finance, institutional fragmentation, divergent national interests, weak institutional and technical capacity, technology and knowledge gaps, and limitations in compliance, transparency and accountability. The findings also showed that climate finance constraints were particularly consequential for vulnerable developing countries, while technological and institutional limitations weakened their capacity to implement climate commitments. The study concluded that the principal challenge facing global climate governance was no longer the absence of international institutional frameworks, but the persistent difficulty of translating commitments into effective domestic implementation and measurable climate outcomes. It recommended an implementation-centred UN climate governance mechanism, reforms to improve equitable and accessible climate finance, stronger institutional and technical capacity in developing countries, enhanced coordination among climate-governance institutions, expanded technology and innovation cooperation, and strengthened transparency and accountability mechanisms.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility, Firm Size, And Tax Aggressiveness in LQ45 Companies
summary: The relationship between corporate social responsibility disclosure, firm size, and tax aggressiveness is examined among companies included in the LQ45 index of the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2021–2024. Secondary data were obtained from audited financial statements, annual reports, and sustainability reports. Purposive sampling produced 25 companies that remained consistently listed and reported profits throughout the observation period, yielding 100 firm-year observations. Tax aggressiveness was represented by the effective tax rate, corporate social responsibility was measured through a 30-item Annexure-A disclosure index, and firm size was calculated using the natural logarithm of total assets. Multiple linear regression was performed with SPSS version 26 after tests of normality, multicollinearity, heteroscedasticity, and autocorrelation. Corporate social responsibility produced a positive but statistically insignificant coefficient toward the effective tax rate, while firm size also produced a positive and insignificant coefficient. The simultaneous test confirmed that both predictors failed to explain tax aggressiveness significantly, with an adjusted coefficient of determination of only 0.3 percent. Intensive social disclosure and substantial asset capacity therefore do not automatically determine the tax behavior of highly visible and liquid firms. The contribution lies in demonstrating the limited explanatory power of disclosure intensity and asset scale within the institutional setting of LQ45 companies

title: FROM SATYAM TO SAHARA: EVOLUTION OF ACCOUNTABILITY MECHANISMS FOR CORPORATE FRAUD IN INDIA
summary: Corporate fraud is among the most serious threats to the integrity, transparency and credibility ofthe Indian corporate sector. Fraudulent financial reporting, diversion of funds, manipulation ofaccounts, misrepresentation of financial information, insider misconduct and failures of corporategovernance harm shareholders, employees, creditors, investors and the wider economy. Thescandals involving Satyam Computer Services Ltd. and the Sahara group offer two instructivereference points for examining how India's accountability framework for corporate fraud hasevolved.The Satyam scandal of January 2009 exposed serious weaknesses in financial reporting, auditing andboard supervision, and prompted a government-led investigation, including scrutiny of the role ofindependent directors and statutory auditors. The Companies Act, 2013 subsequently introducedstronger provisions on fraud, investigation, auditor accountability, independent directors andcorporate governance, and gave statutory status to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO). TheSahara controversy, which unfolded in parallel before SEBI and the Supreme Court and later led toSFIO investigations under Section 212 of the 2013 Act, demonstrated the importance of regulatorycoordination and judicial supervision where the public at large is affected.This paper examines corporate fraud accountability in India under seven heads: (1) introduction; (2)corporate governance as an accountability mechanism; (3) corporate fraud and its forms; (4) theSatyam scandal as a turning point; (5) development of legal and institutional accountabilitymechanisms; (6) critical evaluation, challenges and suggestions; and (7) conclusion. It analyses thetransition from a predominantly reactive enforcement approach towards a framework built onprevention, disclosure, governance, supervision, investigation and judicial accountability, andevaluates the roles of SEBI, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), SFIO, auditors, independentdirectors, stock exchanges, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the courts.

title: Digital Transformation and Green Innovation in Construction Enterprises: The Mediating Role of Green Dynamic Capability and Moderating Effect of Command-and-Control Environmental Regulation
summary: As the digital economy expands rapidly, intelligent-green synergy among construction enterprises has become an inevitable path toward industrial sustainable development, with green innovation acting as its core anchor. Based on the resource-based view, this paper conducts a questionnaire survey on construction enterprises and collects 288 valid questionnaires to empirically examine the influencing mechanism of digital transformation on green innovation in construction enterprises. The results show that the digital transformation of construction enterprises is significantly positively associated with green innovation. Green dynamic capability (GDC) exerts a significant positive mediating effect. Specifically, digital transformation exhibits a positive link with green innovation by enhancing GDC. Meanwhile, command-and-control environmental regulation positively moderates the association between digital transformation and green innovation. Furthermore, a higher level of command-and-control environmental regulation also strengthens the mediating effect transmitted by GDC. Drawing on the above conclusions, this paper proposes suggestions to promote the high-quality development of construction enterprises by deepening green digital transformation, fostering GDC, and leveraging the dividends of command-and-control environmental regulation. The research findings provide theoretical and practical foundations for construction enterprises to seize digital opportunities and fully implement green innovation strategies.

title: Bridging leadership competency gaps across different management levels to enable digital transformation in the construction industry
summary: Purpose As the construction industry undergoes digital transformation, the need for adaptive and effective leadership has become increasingly essential. This study aims to investigate the perceived importance and self-assessed performance of leadership competencies across four management levels in the construction industry. Design/methodology/approach Using survey data collected from 305 construction professionals, 25 leadership competencies were evaluated across four management levels: general staff, line management, middle management and senior management. A refined importance-performance analysis (IPA) approach was applied to identify competency gaps and reveal level-specific leadership patterns. Findings The results show distinct competency gap among different management levels. General staff face significant shortfalls in communication and strategic awareness; line managers underperform in coordination, policy implementation and financial management; middle managers struggle with innovation tolerance and interpreting digital strategies; while senior managers exhibit gaps in digital literacy, team motivation, and market research and evaluation. Originality/value Theoretically, the study contributes to digital transformation research in construction by highlighting the differentiated and multi-level nature of leadership under digital transformation. The findings emphasise leadership development in construction as a dynamic process rather than a static leadership style or set of capabilities. Practically, the study proposes a Multi-level Competency Enablement Pathway to guide leadership development strategies tailored to the specific demands of each management level. The findings provide actionable insights for construction organisations seeking to align leadership capability development with the requirements of digital transformation and enhance organisational digital readiness.

title: Sustainability Reporting Disclosure and Earnings Management: The Role of Board Gender Diversity and Risk Committee Effectiveness
summary: This study investigates how sustainability reporting disclosure relates to earnings management and whether this relationship changes depending on board gender diversity and the effectiveness of the risk committee. Using 590 firm-year observations drawn from Jordanian listed companies, the study estimates the main relationships through pooled ordinary least squares (pooled OLS) regression. The findings indicate a significant negative association between sustainability reporting disclosure and accrual-based earnings management. This suggests that greater sustainability reporting disclosure is associated with less managerial discretion in financial reporting. However, the analysis does not provide statistically significant evidence that board gender diversity or risk committee effectiveness moderates this relationship. The results are robust to alternative earnings management proxies, as similar conclusions are obtained using Kothari-adjusted discretionary accruals and measures of real earnings management. To overcome potential endogeneity and selection issues, additional analyses with the two-step system GMM model yield similar main findings. By focusing on an emerging-market context, the study extends prior research on sustainability and corporate governance and shows that sustainability reporting may serve an important accountability role in strengthening the quality of financial reporting.

title: Transforming the rice–wheat system in India for climate resilience, resource-use efficiency, and food security
summary: The rice–wheat cropping system (RWCS) of the Indo-Gangetic Plains is fundamental to India’s food and nutritional security, accounting for a substantial share of national rice and wheat production while sustaining the livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers. However, decades of intensive cultivation have led to groundwater depletion, soil degradation, declining factor productivity, residue burning, greenhouse gas emissions, and increasing climate vulnerability. This review synthesizes recent advances in technologies, management practices, and institutional innovations for the sustainable transformation of the RWCS. It examines the major biophysical, socio-economic, and policy constraints limiting system performance. The greatest gains in productivity, profitability, resource-use efficiency, and environmental performance arise from integrated production systems that combine improved genetics, conservation agriculture, precision resource management, mechanization, digital technologies, and supportive institutions and policies. Future priorities should focus on scaling proven innovations through efficient seed and machinery delivery systems, climate-smart extension, digital decision support, climate finance, and coordinated water–energy–food governance. Long-term system research integrating agronomic, environmental, economic, and social dimensions will be essential for developing location-specific solutions and informing evidence-based policy. An integrated system approach offers the strongest pathway for enhancing climate resilience, improving resource-use efficiency, reducing environmental footprints, and securing India’s future food and nutritional security.

title: BHDSF v2 - Benghazi Human Digital Safety Framework: Foundations of Human Security in the Digital Transformation Era
summary: This record adds BHDSF Phase II field instrument to Phase I framework (Zenodo, June 2026). Phase I measured 100 students at Shabab Al-Intifada School, Benghazi, showing 48% exposed to digital threats and phishing detection increase from 31% to 81% after gamified intervention. A key gap was exclusion of parents, despite reporting chain "Tell Mom and Dad". title: Agility and Flexibility Strategies in Manufacturing Systems: A Systematic Review with a Focus on Sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Special companies, those in markets with fluctuating demand and supply, need to take the ups and downs in the market, disruption in their supply chains, and the technology and competitive pressure, and still maintain delivery, quality, and cost targets. The present systematic review, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, aims at gathering 42 studies related to the manufacturing agility and flexibility, focusing on Sub Saharan Africa (SSA). The corpus consists of manufacturing flexibility, agile and leagile manufacturing, lean practice, supply-chain agility, digital transformation and Industry 4.0 and is segmented based on application domain, geography, methodology and publication period. The evidence suggests that agility and flexibility are associated with improved operational and organisational performance in SSA, but the pathways and degree of application varies significantly between firms and countries. The consistent challenges are cost, skills, infrastructure (reliability of power supply) and supply chain; management commitment is always cited as the final key. Digital technologies and Industry 4.0 are enablers that require a combination of infrastructure, organisational integration and human capability, and not just ownership of digital technology. There is some fragmentation in measurement of agility – different constructs are used in various surveys, there are formal agility indices, and new AI-assisted assessment frameworks are emerging – none of which have yet been validated for SSA. A series of shop-floor studies in Zimbabwe (process-parameter optimisation, data-driven maintenance, and agent-based condition monitoring) demonstrates that new capabilities at the operational level can be realized at relatively low costs, but are rarely related to the strategic agility literature. The conceptual framework and research agenda of the review call for a SSA-specific measurement tool, an integrated socio-technical model, operational as well as longitudinal evidence, and more robust mechanisms of building industry–academy capabilities, e.g., learning factories.

title: Mediterranean cruise tourism: shore excursions and corporate social responsibility
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how corporate social responsibility (CSR) can be represented as a cybernetic control mechanism within shore excursion systems in Mediterranean cruise tourism. It aims to explore how feedback structures may influence tour operator reputation, environmental sustainability and guest satisfaction in complex destination systems. Design/methodology/approach The study integrates cybernetic theory with system dynamics modelling. A causal loop diagram and stock-and-flow simulation model were developed through Group Model Building and expert-based calibration. Scenario simulations were conducted for three Adriatic cruise destinations – Trieste, Koper and Dubrovnik – to explore system behaviour under different CSR implementation conditions. Findings The simulations illustrate how different configurations of CSR implementation and organisational capabilities may influence system behaviour over time. Within the model, stronger CSR implementation and stakeholder capabilities are associated with reinforcing dynamics linked to reputation, environmental sustainability and guest satisfaction. Research limitations/implications The results should be interpreted as model-generated scenarios rather than empirical predictions. As the model relies on expert-based calibration and destination-specific assumptions, future research should incorporate broader empirical data sets and test the framework in different cruise tourism contexts. Practical implications The model provides a scenario-testing and decision-support tool that can help destination managers, tour operators and policymakers evaluate alternative CSR strategies, identify potential trade-offs and anticipate long-term system responses. Originality/value This study contributes primarily at the methodological level by integrating cybernetic theory, system dynamics modelling, group model building and expert-based calibration into a coherent framework for analysing CSR dynamics in cruise tourism and shore excursion management.

title: Digital Fraud And Online Financial Crimes In India: A Criminological Perspective
summary: The expansion of India’s digital economy has brought about a significant transformation in the financial landscape, particularly through the introduction and widespread adoption of platforms such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), mobile banking systems, and various fintech innovations.[1] These developments have undoubtedly strengthened financial inclusion and contributed to. However, at the same time, they have also created new vulnerabilities, leading to a noticeable rise in digital fraud and online financial crimes.[2] In the recent years, the nature of cybercrime in India has undergone a visible shift. Instead of relying primarily on technical intrusion or hacking, offenders increasingly depend on social engineering, psychological manipulation, and organized criminal networks rather than purely technical hacking.[3] Empirical evidence provided by the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) supports this observation. Cybercrime cases have risen sharply, reaching 86,420 cases in 2023.[4] Particularly important aspect of this data is that nearly 68.9 percent of these offences are fraud-related, which clearly reflects a structural transformation in the nature of cybercrime in India.[5] This research paper adopts a criminological perspective to examine digital fraud in India. It focuses on understanding offender behavior, pattern of victimization and institutional challenges that contribute to the persistence of such crimes. In addition, the paper evaluates the existing legal framework and the effectiveness of regulatory and enforcement mechanisms. The study also examines emerging trends, including digital arrest scams, mule account networks, investment fraud, and data-driven cyber offences.[6] It argues that digital should not be understood merely as a technological issue but rather as a socio-economic and behavioral phenomenon. The paper ultimately concludes that addressing cybercrime in India requires a comprehensive approach that combines legal reform, technological safeguards, improved forensic capacity, and greater public awareness. title: Sustainability Accounting in the 21st Century Economy
summary: This study explores literature survey approach with content search analysis on existing reports, research papers and publications bordering on Sustainability Accounting and the theoretical foundations and applications of Sustainability Accounting in modern economic systems. Grounded in stakeholder theory, legitimacy theory, institutional theory and normative theory, the study underscores how Sustainability Accounting expands the scope of Traditional Accounting to include Environmental, Social, Governance and Economic (ESG-E) metrics. Reporting frameworks such as the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), and the European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) illustrate the institutionalization of sustainability practices and reflect the growing demand for transparency and accountability. The study revealed that Sustainability Accounting is essential for promoting responsible business conduct and sustainable development and that for businesses to be relevant with greater market share, the non-financial reporting aspect (ESG report) should be taken seriously as it enhances the credibility, reliability and acceptability of the financial reporting aspect (Economic report) in the 21st century economy. As economies become more interdependent and sustainability risks intensify, the integration of nonfinancial reporting into mainstream accounting practices is not just beneficial, it is imperative. Thus, the study concludes that Sustainability Accounting advances accounting thought by recognizing the interconnectedness of environmental, social, governance and economic performance.

title: O'zbekistonda sun'iy intellekt texnologiyalarini joriy etish sharoitida inson kapitalining raqamli iqtisodiyot rivojlanishiga ta'sirini ekonometrik baholash
summary: The article econometrically assesses the impact of human capital on the development of Uzbekistan's digital economy under the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, using data for 2010-2024. A three-component composite digital economy index (DEI) is constructed, and human capital is proxied by tertiary enrolment. Autoregressive distributed lag (ADL) models are estimated with Newey-West (HAC) standard errors, including a regime dummy and an interaction term for the AI policy period. The long-run effect of human capital on the DEI is 0.460; its effect on ICT service exports was statistically insignificant before 2021, while in the AI policy period the short-run elasticity reached 1.04 and the long-run elasticity 1.46. Policy proposals for enriching human capital with AI competencies are developed.

title: ETHICAL HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CORPORATE REPUTATION IN THE ERA OF SOCIAL ACCOUNTABILITY: A REVIEW
summary: In an era defined by heightened social accountability, stakeholder scrutiny, and strict Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) mandates, human resource management (HRM) has transitioned from an operational support function to a central ethical driver of corporate reputation. This systematic review synthesizes 16 peer-reviewed benchmark empirical and theoretical studies published between 2021 and 2026 to critically evaluate the mechanisms through which ethical HRM practices influence internal and external corporate reputation. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, literature was extracted across major databases including Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Emerald Insight. The synthesis reveals that ethical HRM—operationalized through procedural justice, fair compensation, whistleblowing protections, inclusive DEI practices, and employee well-being—drives corporate reputation primarily through organizational trust, psychological safety, and perceived authenticity. Structural path meta-evidence demonstrates significant direct and mediated relationships between ethical HRM capabilities and external reputation metrics (R² = 0.62). However, implementation paradoxes such as ethical decoupling, greenwashing/ethics-washing, and algorithmic bias in AI-driven HR tools represent major threats to organizational legitimacy. This review provides an integrative socio-technical framework for organizational leaders and establishes priority directions for future empirical inquiry.

title: Impact of Data Analytics Adoption on Audit Quality in the Public Sector Accounting Reporting
summary: This study investigates the impact of data analytics adoption on audit quality within the context of public sector accounting reporting in Nigeria, focusing specifically on federal government owned tertiary institutions. Drawing on survey data from 98 audit professionals across 130 institutions, the research employs quantitative analysis, including T-tests, to evaluate the effects of data analytics on key dimensions of audit quality: timeliness of financial reporting, audit risk assessment, and resource allocation efficiency. The findings reveal that data analytics significantly enhances the timeliness and accuracy of financial statement reporting, improves the effectiveness of risk assessments, and optimizes resource allocation in audit processes. Despite these positive outcomes, challenges such as limited digital infrastructure and skill gaps among auditors persist. The study concludes that the adoption of data analytics in public sector accounting reporting significantly enhances audit quality by improving the timeliness of financial reporting, strengthening risk assessment, and optimizing resource allocation, thereby fostering greater transparency and accountability in Nigeria’s federal government-owned tertiary institutions. It is therefore, recommended that federal government owned tertiary institutions in Nigeria invest in continuous auditor training, robust technological infrastructure, and supportive regulatory frameworks to fully leverage data analytics for enhanced audit quality and improved public sector financial reporting.

title: Internal Control as a Mechanism Linking Digital Accounting and Financial Reporting Quality in Nigerian SMEs
summary: ABSTRACT: Digital accounting systems can improve accounting processes, but the organisational value of adoption may depend on how system capabilities interact with internal controls. This study qualitatively explores how SME owners, managers and accountants describe internal control as a mechanism linking digital accounting adoption and financial reporting quality in Lagos State, Nigeria. Thirteen participants were purposively selected from a larger survey of 207 SMEs to provide variation in digital adoption, firm size, sector, internal control effectiveness and financial reporting quality. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. Participants consistently described digital accounting systems as strengthening internal controls through audit trails, segregation of duties, approval workflows, exception reporting and standardised procedures. They also associated stronger controls with improvements in the accuracy, timeliness, reliability and completeness of financial reports. A further theme distinguished more extensive use of dedicated accounting systems from limited use of spreadsheets or unconfigured system features. The findings provide qualitative evidence of a pathway consistent with the proposed mediation model, while recognising that qualitative accounts cannot statistically establish mediation or causal effects. The study contributes by showing how control capabilities are experienced in practice and by developing the concept of shallow adoption as limited use of available accounting-system capabilities. The findings suggest that SME digitalisation programmes should combine software provision with control configuration, staff training and monitoring. Keywords: digital accounting; internal control; financial reporting quality; SMEs; technology adoption.
