title: The Effect of Audit Quality, Tenure Audit, And Auditor Reputation On Fraudulent Financial Reporting with Institutional Ownership As A Moderation Variable in Industrial Companies Listed on the IDX For The 2021-2025 Period
summary: This study aims to analyze the effect of audit quality, audit tenure, and auditor reputation on fraudulent financial reporting, with institutional ownership as a moderating variable in industrial sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) for the period 2021–2025. This study employs a quantitative approach using secondary data from audited financial statements and annual reports. The population consists of all industrial sector companies listed on the IDX, and purposive sampling yielded 49 companies or 245 firm-year observations. Fraudulent financial reporting is measured using the Beneish M-Score, audit quality is proxied by the natural logarithm of audit fees, audit tenure is measured by the length of the auditor-client engagement, auditor reputation is measured by a Big Four dummy variable, and institutional ownership is measured by the percentage of shares held by institutional investors. Data were analyzed using panel data regression with Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA), with model selection through the Chow Test and Hausman Test. The results show that audit quality has a significant negative effect on fraudulent financial reporting (β = -0.284, p < 0.001); audit tenure has a significant positive effect (β = 0.157, p < 0.01); auditor reputation has a significant negative effect (β = -0.312, p < 0.001); and institutional ownership significantly strengthens the negative effect of audit quality (interaction β = -0.146, p < 0.01) and weakens the positive effect of audit tenure on fraudulent financial reporting (interaction β = -0.119, p < 0.05). These findings indicate that audit quality and auditor reputation are important mechanisms for detecting and preventing fraudulent financial reporting, and this role is strengthened by the presence of institutional ownership as an external monitoring mechanism

title: Sustainable Finance and the Reallocation of Capital for Ecological Transition
summary: This paper examines the role of sustainable finance in supporting green investment and financing the ecological transition. It reviews three interconnected dimensions: the integration of environmental, social and governance criteria into investment decisions and asset pricing; the development of green financial instruments and financial intermediation; and the financing mechanisms supporting renewable energy, public green investment and corporate transition. The literature indicates that sustainability considerations increasingly affect investor behavior, capital allocation, risk assessment and financing costs, although their financial consequences remain heterogeneous across markets and institutional settings. ESG information can redirect investment flows, but disagreements among rating providers and differences in materiality limit the reliability of sustainability signals. Green bonds, green credit and sustainable banking mechanisms can facilitate environmental investment, yet their effectiveness depends on certification, disclosure quality, liquidity, policy credibility and borrower characteristics. Public financial institutions also play an important role in absorbing early-stage risks, creating markets and mobilizing private capital for low-carbon technologies. The reviewed evidence further shows that climate transition requires more than specialized green instruments. Financial-system structure, corporate investment decisions, regulatory frameworks and coordinated public policies influence whether capital is effectively redirected toward environmentally sustainable activities. Sustainable finance therefore represents an evolving institutional framework through which environmental objectives, financial risk and long-term investment are progressively integrated.

title: Semantic reconfiguration of English technology terms in contemporary Uzbek online media
summary: This article examines how English technology terms are semantically reconfigured in contemporary Uzbek online media. The study does not treat borrowing as a simple transfer of stable dictionary meanings; instead, it focuses on how media context selects, narrows, broadens, or metaphorically extends technological senses after they enter Uzbek discourse. A qualitative sample of ten Uzbek-language media texts published by Spot and O‘zA between 2024 and 2026 is analyzed. Particular attention is paid to platforma, ilova, bulut, startap, bot, model, and trafik. The analysis distinguishes direct lexical borrowing from semantic calquing and local reweighting of an already polysemous English term. The findings show that Uzbek media often institutionalizes technological vocabulary by linking it to public services, education, fintech, artificial intelligence, and platform-based communication. The most visible changes involve metaphorical extension, domain-specific narrowing, and a shift from concrete technical reference to broader service or project meanings.

title: Analisis Kesesuaian Pembiayaan Musyarakah dengan Prinsip Keuangan dalam Islam di PT BPR Syariah Meru Nusantara Mandiri (BNU Syariah)
summary: Musyarakah financing is one of the partnership-based financing schemes in Islamic banking that emphasizes the principles of justice, transparency, profit and loss sharing, and risk sharing. However, its implementation often faces challenges related to business monitoring, financial reporting, and customers' understanding of Islamic financing principles. This study aims to analyze the implementation of the musyarakah contract at PT BPR Syariah Meru Nusantara Mandiri from the perspective of Islamic finance principles. This research employed a qualitative approach with a field research design. Primary data were collected through observations, semi-structured interviews with bank officers, and documentation, while secondary data were obtained from regulations, DSN-MUI Fatwas, books, and relevant scientific literature. The collected data were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, consisting of data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings reveal that the implementation of the musyarakah contract has generally complied with Islamic principles and the DSN-MUI Fatwa No. 08/DSN-MUI/IV/2000 concerning Musyarakah Financing. The principles of justice, transparency, sharia compliance, profit and loss sharing, and risk sharing have been implemented in financing activities. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, including limited financial literacy among customers, inadequate business financial records, and constraints in monitoring financing activities. Therefore, strengthening customer education, improving monitoring systems, and optimizing financial reporting are essential to enhance the effectiveness and sustainability of musyarakah financing.

title: Green accounting and governance capability configurations for sustainability performance in resource constrained environmental governance
summary: Environmental governance research suggests that well-designed sustainability practices can strengthen organizational resilience. Yet public institutions and communities under institutional scarcity may be unable to develop all desirable technological, financial, and managerial capabilities simultaneously. Drawing on Resource Orchestration Theory (ROT), this study examines how Green Accounting, Social Capital, Digital Capability, and Governance Agility combine in relation to Sustainability Performance. Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) of questionnaire data from 152 respondents in Kendari City, Indonesia, identifies three configurations that satisfy the stated sufficiency-retention criteria (primary solution consistency = 0.868; coverage = 0.714) and one additional digital-absence pattern with borderline PRI consistency (0.695), which is treated as exploratory rather than as part of the primary solution. The fully integrated configuration has the highest raw coverage (0.539). Governance Agility narrowly crosses the conventional necessity benchmark (consistency = 0.907; coverage = 0.774), but this near-threshold result is sample-specific; no condition is sufficient alone. Alternative Triple Bottom Line weights produce primary-solution coverage of 0.712–0.715 and consistency of 0.864–0.872. The findings provide a bounded refinement of ROT by treating institutional scarcity as a contextual constraint on feasible capability orchestration and by distinguishing complementary from functionally compensatory capability alignment. Compensation denotes overlapping governance functions, not universal resource substitution. The results support contextual inference for Kendari and require comparison, rather than direct generalization, in other institutional environments.

title: A Study on North-South Rule Conflicts in the Global Climate Governance System
summary: Frequent extreme climate events across the globe underscore the urgency of the global climate governance system. Within the current global climate governance system centered on the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), several principles and mechanisms coexist: differentiated responsibilities, Kyoto flexibility mechanisms, and the Paris Agreement’s Global Stocktake. Nevertheless, divergences persist between developed and developing countries regarding the delineation of historical responsibilities, guarantee of financial inputs, transfer of green technologies, and the right to development. Some unilateral climate measures have prompted debate about their compatibility with multilateral frameworks, which may widen the North-South trust gap and fragments the global climate governance system. After analyzing the dilemmas embedded in the existing governance regime, this paper proposes three pathways for reforming the global climate governance system: accelerating the establishment of a more equitable accounting system, strengthening the coordination and binding force of existing rules, and promptly addressing the shortfalls in finance and technology transfer.

title: Stakeholder-Centric Corporate Social Responsibility: Creating Shared Value Through Strategic Engagement
summary: The notion of corporate social responsibility (CSR) has evolved from an ancillary activity of philanthropy to a strategic approach towards building trust, reputation, and relationship with stakeholders. This research examines the perception of CSR awareness, perceived authenticity, stakeholder engagement, and creation of shared value, and its associations with the variables of trust, reputation, satisfaction/loyalty and behavioral intentions. The data collection instrument comprised 24 items in Likert-type scale form and measured eight variables. The reliability of the measures was checked using Cronbach's alpha, while the Pearson correlation, ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, one-way ANOVA, and independent sample t-test were used for statistical analysis. All Cronbach's alphas fell within the range .67 to .77, showing acceptable reliability, and construct means ranged from 3.52 to 3.70. However, none of the proposed hypotheses was supported, since correlations were weak and statistically insignificant (|r| < .13), and explained less than 4% of variance in satisfaction/loyalty and behavioral intentions (all p > .50). Satisfaction and loyalty significantly differed among different age groups (p = .023), with younger respondents expressing greater satisfaction and loyalty, while there was marginally significant gender difference in stakeholder engagement (p = .085). title: Stakeholder-Centric Corporate Social Responsibility: Creating Shared Value Through Strategic Engagement
summary: The notion of corporate social responsibility (CSR) has evolved from an ancillary activity of philanthropy to a strategic approach towards building trust, reputation, and relationship with stakeholders. This research examines the perception of CSR awareness, perceived authenticity, stakeholder engagement, and creation of shared value, and its associations with the variables of trust, reputation, satisfaction/loyalty and behavioral intentions. The data collection instrument comprised 24 items in Likert-type scale form and measured eight variables. The reliability of the measures was checked using Cronbach's alpha, while the Pearson correlation, ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, one-way ANOVA, and independent sample t-test were used for statistical analysis. All Cronbach's alphas fell within the range .67 to .77, showing acceptable reliability, and construct means ranged from 3.52 to 3.70. However, none of the proposed hypotheses was supported, since correlations were weak and statistically insignificant (|r| < .13), and explained less than 4% of variance in satisfaction/loyalty and behavioral intentions (all p > .50). Satisfaction and loyalty significantly differed among different age groups (p = .023), with younger respondents expressing greater satisfaction and loyalty, while there was marginally significant gender difference in stakeholder engagement (p = .085). There were no significant differences by any other demographic variable or stakeholder type.

title: Underground Coal Mine Fires in Dhanbad, Jharkhand: A Need for Comprehensive State Legislation to Protect the Right to Life and Environment
summary: The underground coal mine fires in the Jharia Coalfield of Dhanbad, Jharkhand, constitute one of India’s longest-running environmental and humanitarian crises. Burning continuously for over a century, these fires have caused extensive environmental degradation, air pollution, land subsidence, destruction of valuable coal reserves, and widespread displacement of local communities. Continuous exposure to toxic gases and particulate matter has resulted in serious public health concerns, including respiratory diseases, cardiovascular disorders, and other chronic illnesses, thereby threatening the fundamental right to life and a healthy environment guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Although several central enactments, including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and the Mines Act, 1952, provide a general framework for environmental protection and mining regulation, they do not adequately address the unique challenges posed by underground coal mine fires. This article critically examines the constitutional and statutory obligations of the Union and the State Governments in preventing mine fires, protecting public health, ensuring environmental restoration, and rehabilitating affected communities. It argues that the absence of a comprehensive state-specific legal framework has contributed to fragmented governance and ineffective implementation of existing policies. The article proposes the enactment of a dedicated Jharkhand Underground Coal Mine Fire Prevention, Rehabilitation and Environmental Protection Act, establishing an independent statutory authority for fire prevention, environmental monitoring, scientific risk assessment, rehabilitation, compensation, and inter-agency coordination. Adopting a doctrinal research methodology based on constitutional provisions, statutory analysis, judicial precedents, government reports, and secondary literature, the article concludes that comprehensive state legislation is essential to uphold environmental justice, strengthen environmental governance, protect public health, ensure accountable rehabilitation, and secure the rights of present and future generations.

title: Resisting or transforming? Workforce readiness for digital shift in healthcare workflows
summary: Purpose This study examines the effect of digital literacy on operational efficiency, with technology acceptance and readiness for digital transformation as mediating variables. It also investigates the moderating role of workload pressure and resistance to change in the relationship between digital literacy and readiness for digital transformation, to better understand the factors influencing successful digital transformation in organizations. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design with a cross-sectional survey was adopted. Data were collected from 105 frontline professionals working in a tertiary-care hospital and research centre in South Karnataka, India, representing a fast-digitizing yet resource-constrained healthcare sector. Six constructs were measured using a structured questionnaire, and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test reliability, structural relationships, mediation and moderation effects. Findings The results show that digital literacy significantly enhances technology acceptance and readiness for digital transformation, which in turn improves operational efficiency. Technology acceptance mediates the relationship between digital literacy and readiness. However, workload pressure and resistance to change did not significantly moderate the relationship, indicating that the positive effect of digital literacy on readiness remains stable even under high workload and resistance conditions in the hospital setting. Research limitations/implications The findings guide hospital administrators and policymakers on the importance of digital training, inclusive leadership and change management to support staff readiness and improve hospital efficiency during digital transitions. Practical implications The findings highlight the need for structured digital training and effective change-management practices to improve efficiency and performance in hospitals. Originality/value The study extends the Technology Acceptance Model by linking digital literacy and technology acceptance to operational performance and provides empirical evidence on workforce readiness in an emerging tertiary healthcare context.

title: The Substantive Impact of the UK "Say on Pay" Regime on Executive Compensation Levels
summary: This paper examines the substantive impact of the UK “say on pay” regime on executive compensation levels. It first outlines the regime’s legislative development, dual-track information disclosure system and two-tier shareholder voting mechanism consisting of binding votes on remuneration policies and advisory votes on implementation reports. The study finds that the regime has failed to curb the sustained growth of total executive compensation, yet it has promoted the shift of pay structure towards a performance-oriented model and expanded the application of long-term incentive plans, while strong shareholder opposition can drive targeted pay adjustments in individual cases. The paper further attributes the limited effectiveness to internal corporate governance flaws, the non-binding nature of most voting outcomes and structural problems in shareholding. Finally, it puts forward targeted reform proposals, concluding that further institutional improvements are required to better align executive pay with corporate performance.

title: The Effect of Real Earnings Management, Institutional Ownership, and Other Factors on Firm Value in Indonesia
summary: This study aims to obtain empirical evidence on the effect of institutional ownership, audit committee, real earnings management, profitability, liquidity, firm size, tax avoidance, and independent board of commissioners on firm value. The sample consists of 108 manufacturing companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during 2022 to 2024, resulting in 324 observations. Using a quantitative approach with purposive sampling and multiple regression analysis, the results show that profitability and the independent board of commissioners have a positive effect on firm value, while real earnings management and liquidity have a negative effect. Meanwhile, institutional ownership, audit committee, firm size, and tax avoidance have no effect on firm value.

title: Strategies adopted by construction firms to overcome the challenges of adopting Industry 4.0: an Australian perspective
summary: Purpose Industry 4.0 (I4.0) presents a significant potential for digital transformation in the construction industry (CI), yet a substantial implementation gap remains. Despite digital advancements in Australian CI, many firms struggle to translate digital potential into operational outcomes. Existing studies largely catalogue adoption barriers but provide limited, actionable guidance on how to move forward. This study aims to address this gap by identifying practical, firm-led strategies to overcome these challenges within the Australian context. Design/methodology/approach Using purposive and snowball sampling, 19 semi-structured interviews were conducted with directors, managers, innovation officers and other personnel experienced in implementing I4.0-related technologies (I4.0-tech) in their firms. These interviews were analysed using content analysis techniques. Findings Drawing on the technology-organisation-environment framework, the study identifies technical limitations, organisational resistance and relational deficiencies as key inhibitors of I4.0 adoption. A dual-layered response is needed, comprising formalised governance to drive change management and empirical validation to demonstrate job-specific value. Successful integration also relies on top-down leadership to build a digital culture, unified standards and strategic partnerships that support collaborative risk mitigation and resource sharing. Originality/value To build upon established I4.0 implementation strategies, this study anchors its contribution in the practical realities of the Australian construction industry. The research advances current understanding by isolating specific, practitioner-based mechanisms for digital adoption. Grounded in these findings, this study offers an empirical lessons-learned repository with practical insights for managing and navigating the industry’s digital transformation.

title: Mechanism of Rule Alignment between the Hainan Free Trade Port and ASEAN
summary: Rule alignment between the Hainan Free Trade Port and ASEAN is a dynamic governance process in which different rule systems move from coexistence toward compatibility under conditions of institutional heterogeneity. Building on the conceptualization of rule alignment and the “institutional interface,” this paper constructs an analytical framework of “factor flows—actor coordination—institutional diffusion” from the perspectives of institutional complexity and cross-domain collaborative governance, and examines the practical forms of alignment in such fields as goods trade, investment and trade in services, personnel qualifications, and the digital economy. The study finds that cross-border factor flows continuously render institutional frictions visible and generate demands for alignment; multiple governance actors form rule connections through coordinated interaction; and functional platforms drive the diffusion of institutional innovation through pilot experimentation. Current problems include bias in demand identification, fragmentation of actor coordination, and insufficient transformation of pilot outcomes. The effectiveness of rule alignment should therefore be improved through demand feedback, tiered coordination, and evaluation-diffusion mechanisms.

title: Control interno y gestión de riesgos financieros: revisión bibliométrica y síntesis temática con implicaciones conceptuales para el sector cooperativo
summary: The objective of this study was to analyze the evolution and conceptual structure of the scientific literature identified at the explicit intersection of internal control and financial risk, and to synthesize its conceptual implications for credit unions. A literature review was conducted using a quantitative approach with a descriptive-bibliometric scope. Data were obtained from Scopus using the TITLE-ABS-KEY search equation (“financial risk” AND “internal control”), applied on July 4, 2026, to articles published through 2026. The identification and selection process was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and resulted in a final corpus of 64 articles published between 1991 and 2026. The analysis incorporated temporal evolution, bibliometric mapping using PHAROS METRIX NEXT, and a thematic synthesis of the 64 records. The results showed a recent expansion of the field: 39 articles (60.9%) were concentrated between 2024 and 2026. The conceptual framework revealed recurring links between financial risk, internal control, corporate governance, auditing, financial reporting, fraud, digital transformation, and sustainability. The integrative synthesis, compared with the COSO framework, organized the evidence into four dimensions: control and governance environment; comprehensive risk identification and measurement; control, audit, and remediation activities; and information, technology, and communication. These dimensions are not presented as an empirically validated model, but rather as a conceptual adaptation that facilitates the prudent transfer of heterogeneous findings to the cooperative sector. It is concluded that the literature offers a useful basis for guiding future research and the design of control and risk management systems in cooperatives, without constituting direct evidence of effectiveness in these entities.

title: Contributing to SDGs 9, 16, and 17: Unveiling the Role of Supply Chain Analytics, Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management and Trust
summary: ABSTRACT The primary objective of this study is to explore the relationships between supply chain (SC) analytics, cybersecurity supply chain risk management (C‐SCRM), SC trust, and Sustainable Development goals (SDGs) in a sample of Jordanian pharmaceutical SCs, considered an emerging country. To test the aforementioned relationships, a conceptual research model was designed to frame these relationships based on both information processing theory (IPT) and dynamic capabilities view (DCV). To empirically test the model, a questionnaire was developed and distributed as a measurement tool. Based on 224 responses, the data were analyzed using partial least squares‐structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM). It was concluded that the hypotheses were acceptable, that SC analytics positively impacts C‐SCRM, and that C‐SCRM positively impacts SDGs. Finally, the moderating effect of SC trust on the relationship between SC analytics and C‐SCRM was accepted. This study made interesting and meaningful academic and managerial contributions, as well as new, innovative, and fresh insights into how data analytics and cyber risk management systems can be applied in SCs and how these factors can enhance sustainable development.

title: SOP Standardization as a Governance Instrument: Strengthening Governance and Sharia Compliance in Islamic Financial Institutions
summary: This study examines Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) standardization as a governance instrument for strengthening Good Corporate Governance (GCG) and Sharia compliance in Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs). Using a qualitative descriptive-normative literature review, data were drawn from 28 sources (2014–2026) and analyzed through a thematic coding framework, grounded in Agency, Stewardship, and Stakeholder Theory. A comparative case analysis contrasting the procedural breakdown at PT BPRS GP Medan with digitalized SOP practices at Bank Syariah Indonesia and KSPPS Nuri Jatim shows that rigid, automated SOP enforcement rather than manual, discretionary procedures is decisive in preventing Sharia agency fraud. Benchmarking against AAOIFI, IFSB, and Bank Negara Malaysia standards further reveals that Indonesia's predominantly ex-post supervisory model could be strengthened by a more proactive, line-management-based three-lines-of-defense framework. Findings indicate that SOP standardization enhances transparency, accountability, internal control, and Sharia compliance, functioning most effectively when systematically enforced and resistant to manual override. This study offers actionable implications for OJK, IFI management, and the Sharia Supervisory Board (DPS), while acknowledging its reliance on secondary, documentary case evidence rather than primary empirical data.

summary: Separate legal personality allows a company to conduct business in its own name and ordinarilyconfines a shareholder's exposure to the capital committed. The rule associated with Salomon v. A.Salomon & Co. Ltd. remains essential to investment and enterprise, including India's growing startupsector. Yet the rule does not answer every question about wrongdoing carried out through acompany. Indian law may impose an obligation on the company itself, attach responsibility to adirector or promoter under a specific legal provision, or, in exceptional circumstances, look through acorporate structure used to evade the law. These are distinct routes to accountability. This papertraces the development of Indian company law and examines judicial decisions, the Companies Act,2013, insolvency law, and newer regulatory demands affecting technology businesses. It argues thatsound corporate governance depends on identifying the legal basis for liability in each case whileretaining the commercial value of incorporation. Clearer rules and more effective enforcement wouldbetter protect creditors, investors, and the public without treating every business failure as personalmisconduct.

title: Capital Structure Decisions and Financial Performance of Firms Listed in the Alternative Investment Market Segment of the Nairobi Securities Exchange.
summary: Financial performance, reflected in profitability, liquidity and market valuation, is a critical measure of the sustainability and growth of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) listed on the Alternative Investment Market Segment (AIMS) of the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). Despite relaxed listing requirements and tax incentives intended to widen SME access to public capital, AIMS-listed firms continue to face thin market liquidity, high perceived investment risk, limited access to affordable long-term debt and governance gaps, with the segment accounting for less than 5% of total NSE market capitalization and more than 60% of its firms reporting volatile or declining profits between 2019 and 2024. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between capital structure decisions and financial performance among firms listed on AIMS. It specifically examined the influence of debt-based financing, equity-based financing, hybrid financing and retained earnings-based financing on financial performance. The study was anchored on the Static Trade-Off Theory, Agency Cost Theory, Market Timing Theory and Pecking Order Theory. A descriptive and explanatory cross-sectional research design was adopted, targeting all nine AIMS-listed firms through a census, from which five finance and strategic decision-makers per firm were purposively selected, giving a sample of 45 respondents. Primary data were collected using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire and were supplemented with secondary data from audited financial statements. Both descriptive and inferential statistical methods, namely Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis, were used to analyse the data, which were presented in tables and discussed. The findings revealed that the four financing decisions jointly explained 44.8% of the variation in financial performance (F = 3.236, p = 0.027). Hybrid financing had the strongest positive and significant influence on financial performance, followed by debt-based financing, while equity-based financing and retained earnings-based financing had positive and significant but comparatively smaller influences. The study, therefore, recommends that AIMS-listed firms should adopt balanced and well-monitored debt strategies aligned with cash flow capacity, expand equity financing while carefully managing dilution, prioritize hybrid instruments such as convertible securities to enhance flexibility and cost efficiency, and strengthen profit retention and reinvestment policies complemented by external financing.

title: The Effect of Accounting Understanding, Accounting System Utilization, Internal Audit, and Internal Control System on The Quality of Hospital Financial Statements: A Study at PT XYZ
summary: This study investigates the impact of accounting comprehension, the accounting systems utilization, internal audit, and internal control systems on the quality of financial statements at PT XYZ, a state-owned enterprise managing four hospitals and five clinics in East Java. A quantitative research design with an associative approach was employed, with purposive sampling to select respondents. The final samples comprised 35 respondents consisting of accounting and finance staff directly involved in preparing financial statements. Data were collected using questionnaires and analyzed through multiple linear regression. The findings simultaneously indicate that the four independent variables significantly affect the quality of financial statements, with a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.845. Thus, 84.5% of the variation in financial statement quality can be explained by the research model. Partially, accounting comprehension and the accounting systems utilization exert positive but insignificant effects. While internal audit and internal control systems have positive and significant effects, with internal control systems being the most dominant variable. These results underscore that the reliability of hospital financial reporting is more strongly determined by the effectiveness of organizational control and oversight mechanisms than by individual competence alone. This research is perceived to serve as an evaluation material for PT XYZ’s management in strengthening internal control systems and internal audit functions to improve the quality of financial statements sustainably.

title: The One-Way Door: Why Carbon Steelmakers Divest Specialty Steel
summary: Independent analysis of whether carbon and specialty steelmaking belong under one roof. Traces roughly thirty ownership changes across nine countries and five decades, finding that carbon steel majors divest specialty businesses about three times as often as they acquire them — and that only one clean reversal appears in the record. Sets out the technical divergence from melting to rolling, shows how access to capital markets decides whether separation comes through spin-off, bankruptcy or state-directed consolidation, and examines the defence exception, where governments override the market. Closes with practical lessons for boards, investors and governments.

title: A socio-technical mechanism of the agricultural digital divide: Ecuador within a heterogeneous Latin American context
summary: Digital agriculture can improve farm management, resource-use efficiency, and decision-making; however, access to technology alone does not guarantee equivalent economic benefits. This perspective article conceptualizes the agricultural digital divide as a socio-technical and economic inequality that can arise along a sequence linking structural conditions, resource accessibility, capability formation, technological appropriation, productive integration, economic value realization, and value capture and benefit distribution. This definition extends the analysis beyond connectivity and adoption by considering whether agricultural actors can integrate technologies into viable productive activities and retain a significant share of the value generated. Institutions, extension services, cooperatives, financing mechanisms, technology providers, business models, and data governance can shape the transitions between these stages. Ecuador is examined as a focal analytical case within a heterogeneous Latin America, without assuming regional representativeness. The framework redirects the evaluation of digitalization away from the number of technologies deployed and toward their productive appropriation, economic viability, and the distribution of their benefits, thereby reinforcing the relationship between digital transformation and agricultural economics.

title: Reinforcement learning for adaptive supplier sustainability scoring and sourcing share adjustment in ready made garment supply chains
summary: Global supply chains face increasing legal, commercial, and stakeholder pressure to verify supplier sustainability rather than rely only on supplier claims. This study develops a safety-gated tabular Q-learning framework for adaptive supplier scoring, limited sourcing-share adjustment, and audit targeting in a stylized Bangladesh ready-made garment sourcing portfolio. The simulation distinguishes direct exporters, subcontractors, and small or informal suppliers; represents safety, labour, and environmental performance separately; prohibits rewards when verified safety or labour falls below 0.60; and imposes a minimum annual audit. Three independently trained agents were evaluated in 75 paired out-of-sample replications against a contextual bandit, a risk-based adaptive heuristic, a static threshold, a combined scheduled-audit-and-threshold policy, scheduled auditing, and random action. Q-learning achieved mean true compliance of 0.862 compared with 0.820 under the static threshold, increased the share of suppliers at or above 0.80 from 58.2 to 81.3%, and reduced mean severe incidents from 3.29 to 1.71. It used 167 audits compared with 362 for the combined scheduled-audit-and-threshold policy, a 53.8% reduction, while mean procurement cost was 1.1% higher than under the static threshold. The contextual bandit produced lower compliance (0.742) and more incidents (2.96), supporting the value of delayed-action learning. The risk-based heuristic produced statistically similar mean compliance but required 55 additional audits and yielded a narrower compliant-supplier share. Paired tests, effect sizes, convergence diagnostics, supplier-stratum results, credit-assignment ablation, time-state testing, and multi-parameter robustness analyses are reported. The findings remain simulation evidence rather than factory-level validation, but they provide a reproducible and technically strengthened test of adaptive supplier governance.

title: Examining the Impact of Corporate Social Responsibility on Financial Performance: Evidence from Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises in Hanoi
summary: This study examines the effect of corporate social responsibility (CSR) on the financial performance (FP) of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Hanoi, Vietnam, through the mediating role of corporate reputation (REP). Drawing on stakeholder theory, signaling theory, the resource-based view, legitimacy theory, and the creating-shared-value perspective, CSR is conceptualized using Turker's (2009) four-dimension, stakeholder-based scale — CSR toward social and non-social stakeholders, employees, customers, and government. Survey data were collected from 300 owners/managers of SMEs operating in Hanoi and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 3, with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) and blindfolding procedures. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity (Cronbach's alpha 0.752-0.875; AVE 0.625 0.728; HTMT below 0.85), corroborated by exploratory factor analysis (KMO = 0.887; six factors, 67.03% variance explained). Results show that all four CSR dimensions positively and significantly influence REP (β = 0.133-0.298, p < 0.01), and REP in turn is the strongest predictor of FP (β = 0.469, p < 0.001), fully mediating the CSR-FP relationship as specified in the model. Firm size is the only significant control variable. CSR toward social/non-social stakeholders exerts the strongest effect, while CSR toward government exerts the weakest, a pattern explained through legitimacy theory as a "hygiene-factor" effect. The study contributes cross-cultural validation of Turker's scale in an emerging-economy SME context and offers evidence-based, prioritized managerial recommendations for CSR investment under resource constraints.

title: Enhancing Public Accountability through IPSAS-Based Financial Reporting: Evidence from the Turkish Court of Accounts
summary: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether financial reporting compliant with Public Accounting Standards prepared based on IPSAS enhances accountability in the public sector, through the perceptions of auditors at the Turkish Court of Accounts (TCA). Reform approaches such as new public management and new public financial management have accelerated the transition to the accrual basis in public accounting and the development of International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS). In line with this global trend, Türkiye transitioned to an accrual-based accounting system under the Public Financial Management and Control Law No. 5018, and subsequently published the Public Accounting Standards prepared based on IPSAS. Data were collected via a survey administered between March and July 2021 to 111 professional auditors at the TCA and analyzed using exploratory factor analysis and multiple linear regression. The empirical findings indicate that, according to TCA auditor perceptions, standards-compliant financial reporting is positively associated with accountability. However, the perception that full compliance with PAS had not yet been achieved in public institutions during the 2021 data collection period indicates an implementation gap between the potential benefits of the standards and the level of implementation during the reform process.

title: Executive compensation, strategic investment, productivity, and firm performance
summary: Executive compensation design is central to corporate governance. Pay contracts may shape managers’ incentives to undertake investments with delayed returns. This paper analyzes how the equity-based and long-term component of CEO compensation relates to strategic investment, productivity, and operating performance among U.S. public firms covered by Compustat and ExecuComp over 1992–2017. We estimate a recursive generalized structural equation model linking the share of equity-based and long-term compensation (EB-LT) to R&D expenditure, advertising expenditure, Levinsohn–Petrin total factor productivity, and EBITDA, and examine CEO firm-specific tenure as a moderator. A 10-percentage-point higher EB-LT share is associated with 11.4% higher R&D spending and 8.9% higher advertising spending. R&D and advertising are, in turn, strongly related to productivity, and productivity is positively related to EBITDA. The findings identify a structured compensation–investment–productivity–performance nexus in which EB-LT compensation is most consistently connected to strategic investment channels. They also suggest that equity-based incentive design should be evaluated jointly with firms’ investment strategies, productivity outcomes, and CEO tenure profiles, rather than viewed in isolation as a mechanism for improving productivity or profits.

title: Mechanism of anti-crisis financial management of an insurance company amidst cyberattacks and digital shocks
summary: The article provides a theoretical generalization and develops a practical mechanism for the anti-crisis financial management of an insurance company amidst the growing intensity of cyberattacks and resulting digital shocks. The study analyzes the contemporary operating environment of the Ukrainian insurance market, characterized by high military-economic uncertainty, strict regulatory oversight by the National Bank of Ukraine on compliance with capital and solvency requirements, and accelerated digitalization of business processes. The widespread adoption of online sales and automated claims settlement, alongside business advantages, has created high technological dependence and qualitatively new threats to insurers’ financial stability. The study aims to substantiate the conceptual foundations and develop a comprehensive anti-crisis mechanism for an insurance company’s financial management to ensure its liquidity, solvency, and operational continuity under conditions of digital shocks. In the research process, a set of scientific methods was applied: systemic, structural-functional, and comparative analysis – to examine the impact factors of the digital environment and assess the limitations of traditional anti-crisis management approaches; statistical, economic-mathematical, and graphical analysis—to study the dynamics, structure, and vectors of cyberattacks on the financial sector of Ukraine in 2025; and scientific modeling—to develop the multi-level architecture of the anti-crisis mechanism. The results confirm that the financial sector remains a primary target for cybercriminals, with malware distribution, phishing, and account compromise as the main tools. It was established that classic anti-crisis management instruments, focused on retrospective ratio analysis, static reserves, and standard budgeting, prove ineffective against the high velocity of digital shock propagation, which can trigger immediate cash gaps, premium inflow disruption, and reputational damage. The research’s scientific novelty lies in developing an author-designed adaptive mechanism for anti-crisis financial management, enabling a qualitative shift from passive loss coverage to proactively building an insurer’s digital resilience. The novelty comprises measures structured across three temporal and functional levels: the preventive level involves establishing an early warning system for digital crises and modeling combined cyber scenarios within solvency stress testing; the operational level encompasses forming a targeted reserve for financial adaptation and cyber resilience along with dynamic management of highly liquid assets; the strategic level is based on cyber risk transfer through reinsurance, IT security cost optimization, and the full integration of cyber risk management into corporate governance. The practical significance of the results is that executive management in insurance companies can directly implement the proposed tools and algorithms to rapidly neutralize digital threats, maintain payment channel continuity, and preserve high customer trust during crises. Future research could develop mathematical models to formalize early-warning indicators of a digital crisis using Artificial Intelligence and Big Data, and refine actuarial calculations to determine the optimal volume of the financial adaptation reserve. title: Monitoring and Evaluation Tools, Stakeholder Involvement and Implementation of Digital Data Systems in the Public Service in Kenya
summary: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to examine the role of monitoring and evaluation tools and stakeholder involvement in the implementation and sustainability of digital data systems in the public service in Kenya. Methodology: The study adopted a literature-based approach to examine existing knowledge on participatory monitoring and evaluation, digital data systems, stakeholder engagement, and project sustainability in the public service. The theoretical framework was guided by the stakeholder participation theories of Arnstein (1969), Burns, Hambleton and Hoggett (1994), and Wilcox (2003). Findings: The study found that effective stakeholder involvement in monitoring and evaluation enhances ownership, accountability, transparency, capacity development, service delivery, and project sustainability. The use of digital technologies facilitates timely data collection, information sharing, performance tracking, feedback, and evidence-based decision-making. However, effective implementation and sustainability may be constrained by inadequate resources, limited technical skills, poor institutional support, resistance to technological change, corruption, political interference, poor data quality, and weak monitoring structures. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The study concludes that integrating appropriate monitoring and evaluation tools with meaningful stakeholder participation and effective digital data systems can strengthen project performance and sustainability in the Kenyan public service. It recommends continuous stakeholder training, inclusive participation throughout the project cycle, regular feedback mechanisms, improved monitoring and evaluation systems, enhanced technical and institutional capacity, and stronger government and institutional support for sustainable digital transformation.

title: When public money speaks: local government special bonds and corporate green innovation in China
summary: Public investment reallocates both resources and expectations. This study examines this dual role through China’s local government special bonds, a project-based fiscal instrument that reveals local governments’ green development priorities through observable and spatially targeted spending commitments. We construct a novel dataset of 146,601 special bond projects from 2019 to 2024, identify county-level allocations to the new-energy sector, and match them with Chinese A-share listed firms. We find that new-energy special bond allocation significantly increases corporate green innovation. The result is robust to alternative measures, Tobit estimation, winsorization, placebo tests using non-green patents, dynamic DID analysis, Bartik instrumental variables, propensity score matching, and entropy balancing. Mechanism tests show that corporate climate risk attention, measured from annual reports, partially mediates the effect, suggesting that targeted public investment guides managerial attention in addition to supplying capital. The effect is stronger where policy signals are more credible or easier to absorb, including regions with developed venture capital markets, carbon pilot cities, and projects using bond funds as capital. Executive green background further strengthens firms’ innovation response. These findings show how place-based public investment transforms fiscal allocation into corporate climate cognition and green innovation.

title: AI-induced corporate social responsibility (AICSR) and e-retailing: a game-changing strategy or a gimmick to attain customer loyalty
summary: Purpose This study examines the direct and mediated effects of AI-induced corporate social responsibility (AICSR) initiatives on customer loyalty in e-retailing, grounded in an integrated theoretical framework of stakeholder theory and signaling theory. It clarifies whether AICSR fosters customer loyalty directly or indirectly via a series of intervening pathways. Design/methodology/approach We tested the framework using cross-sectional survey data collected from 234 active Chinese online retail consumers, and analyzed the dataset via partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4. Findings Results reveal that AICSR exerts a significant positive direct effect on customer loyalty. Meanwhile, its influence is transmitted through six constructs – retailer service quality, customer satisfaction, electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM), retailer image, retailer reputation and customer trust – through both individual mediation pathways and a sequential pathway involving all six mediators. These mediators exhibit significant positive relationships, highlighting their interconnected roles in explaining customer loyalty. Originality/value This study extends extant literature by unpacking the paradox of legitimate distinctiveness amid AICSR in the e-commerce industry. It demonstrates that the effectiveness of AICSR initiatives extends beyond their direct contribution to customer loyalty, revealing the interconnected mechanisms through which AI-induced CSR can generate broader customer value.

title: Climate Risk Disclosure, Green Finance, and Cost of Capital Among PSX Non-Financial Firms
summary: ABSTRACT: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to examine correlations between climate risk disclosure quality (CRDI), green finance (GFI), and cost of capital (COC) among Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX)-based non-financial companies for 2013-2023. The study is based on Information Asymmetry Theory, Stakeholder Theory and Legitimacy Theory to investigate whether superior climate risk disclosure leads to lower cost of equity, debt and WACC; whether green finance acts as a mediator in the context of the aforementioned relationship; and whether board environmental expertise acts as a moderator in the mediated pathway. Design/Methodology/Approach: An unbalanced panel of 165 PSX-listed non-financial firms (maximum 1,815 firm-year observations) is analyzed. The Climate Risk Disclosure Index (CRDI) is a 24-item index based on structured content analysis (dual-coder, Cohen's Kappa = 0.83), which can be disaggregated to include the categories of transition risk disclosure (TRD), physical risk disclosure (PRD), and governance climate accountability (GCA). Cost of equity is calculated by using CAPM, cost of debt by using the interest expense ratio and WACC by using the market-value weighting. Green finance is expressed in a PCA-weighted combination of four instruments. Endogeneity is controlled for using System GMM (Blundell and Bond, 1998). Estimation of mediation (PROCESS Model 4) and moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 14) involves the use of BCa bootstrapped confidence intervals (5000 iterations). Findings: CRDI is negatively and significantly associated with cost of equity (beta = -0.187, p < 0.001), cost of debt (beta = -0.142, p < 0.001), and WACC (beta = -0.168, p < 0.001). The CRDI-cost of equity relationship is partially mediated by green finance (indirect effect = -0.072; BCa 95% CI [-0.118, -0.031]), accounting for nearly 38.5% of the total. Highly-efficient boards (IMM = -0.024; BCa 95% CI [-0.041, -0.009]) provide significant moderation of this mediated pathway, reducing costs by 2.1x more. Other disclosure variables, including transition risk disclosure (beta = -0.214), have higher effects on capital costs than do physical risk disclosure (beta = -0.156). All results are robust to GMM endogeneity correction. Research Limitations: Single-country PSX setting; GRI content-analysis-based CRDI is based on self-disclosed reports; limited data availability on green finance after 2023 for SECP-mandatory PE disclosures; and availability of data for the era before SECP-mandatory PE disclosures is limited. Practical Implications: Ensure that SECP require TCFD related disclosures by PSX companies. To incentivize green finance cost reduction, environmental expertise investment is needed in boards. SBP Sustainable Finance Framework certification is a capital cost optimizing strategy outside of regulation. Originality/Value: It is the first study which provide the TCFD-aligned CRDI for PSX non-financial firms disaggregating TRD, PRD, and GCA; (2) it is the first study to find evidence of CRDI-COC through the mediation of green finance; (3) it is the first study to test Board EE as a moderator; and (4) it is the most comprehensive PSX decade panel climate disclosure and capital costs with System GMM correction. Keywords: climate risk disclosure; green finance; cost of capital; TCFD; board environmental expertise; PSX; WACC; information asymmetry; System GMM; emerging markets

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Supply Chain Management.
summary: This paper investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in supply chain management, highlighting the main challenges and opportunities of its application and developing recommendations for practice. It adopts a qualitative method, an interpretivist philosophy and a deductive approach. Primary data were collected through open-ended interviews with nineteen supply chain managers and analysed using narrative analysis. Secondary data were drawn from peer-reviewed journal articles published since 2012 and analysed thematically. The findings indicate that AI is steadily taking a larger role in the supply chain, improving the accuracy of demand forecasting and order fulfilment. AI-enabled robots and machines also reduce human error and improve workplace safety. However, the energy and cost involved can raise operational investment, and many developers are deterred by the power demands of deep learning. Introducing systems to the workforce early, with equal training for everyone, can significantly speed up adoption. This paper is condensed from an MSc applied dissertation completed at the University of Salford (2021/2022), supervised by Dr Langes Supramaniam.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Demonstration Zone Policies on the Green Innovation Resilience of Manufacturing Firms
summary: Using firm-level panel data from Chinese A-share-listed manufacturing firms over the period 2019–2024, this study exploits the staggered implementation of the National New-Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Development Demonstration Zones as a quasi-natural experiment. A multi-period difference-in-differences (DID) framework is employed to identify the causal effect of AI demonstration zone policies on firms’ green innovation resilience, while further investigating the underlying mechanisms and heterogeneous effects. The empirical results indicate that the establishment of AI demonstration zones significantly strengthens the green innovation resilience of manufacturing firms. This finding remains robust to a series of alternative specifications, placebo tests, and other robustness checks. Mechanism analyses suggest that the policy operates through three complementary channels. First, AI-oriented policy support improves firms’ total factor productivity, enhances their capacity to adapt to changing environments, and thereby improves the efficiency and continuity of green technology innovation. Second, fiscal subsidies and tax incentives associated with the policy help ease financing constraints and mitigate the financial risks inherent in green innovation activities. Third, the policy promotes firms’ substantive green innovation, enabling them to accumulate technological capabilities and reserves that strengthen their ability to respond to environmental regulatory pressures and market uncertainty. Further analysis reveals significant heterogeneity across firms. The positive effect is more pronounced among non-state-owned enterprises, firms facing stronger market competition, and high-tech manufacturing firms. Overall, the findings provide micro-level evidence that AI-oriented development policies can generate broader environmental and innovation benefits beyond their direct technological objectives. They also highlight the potential of digital technology policies to strengthen firms’ capacity to sustain green innovation in the face of regulatory, financial, and market uncertainties, offering relevant implications for developing economies pursuing digital transformation and sustainable development.

title: Digital Search Disruption and Corporate Governance: Evidence From Google's Withdrawal and Executive Gender Diversity in China
summary: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study examines whether disruptions to digital information infrastructure influence corporate governance outcomes. Specifically, it investigates how Google's 2010 withdrawal from mainland China affected executive gender diversity by altering firms' external visibility within global information networks. Research Findings/Insights Using a difference‐in‐differences framework, the study finds that firms with greater prewithdrawal exposure to Google experienced a significant decline in executive gender diversity after the withdrawal. The results remain robust across alternative specifications and identification tests. Mechanism analyses suggest that reductions in foreign media visibility and weakened foreign investor monitoring are important channels, which reduce external governance pressures. Further analyses reveal that the effect is stronger in regions with less supportive gender‐norm environments and greater information‐accessibility constraints, with gender norms showing a more robust moderating role. Theoretical/Academic Implications This study extends corporate governance research by identifying digital information infrastructure as an important governance‐relevant information intermediary. The findings broaden existing perspectives beyond traditional disclosure and monitoring mechanisms by showing that governance outcomes are also shaped by the infrastructures that determine firms' visibility and accessibility to external stakeholders. The study further demonstrates that executive gender diversity responds not only to internal organizational choices but also to changes in firms' external informational environments. Practitioner/Policy Implications The findings highlight the importance of maintaining reliable and accessible digital information infrastructures that support external accountability mechanisms. Firms should treat digital visibility as a strategic governance resource and develop diversified channels to maintain stakeholder connections when key information infrastructures are disrupted.

title: Digital Transformation in Banking and Financial Performance of Commercial Banks in Uasin Gishu County, Kenya.
summary: Digital banking adoption refers to the integration and use of electronic platforms such as mobile banking, internet banking, agency banking and automated teller machines (ATMs) to deliver financial services. It is increasingly regarded as a critical driver of efficiency, service delivery and financial performance in the banking sector. Global evidence shows that digital banking usage exceeds 70% in advanced markets, while in Kenya over 80% of banking transactions are now conducted through digital channels. However, financial performance across commercial banks remains uneven owing to disparities in digital infrastructure, cybersecurity risks, high technology investment costs and uneven adoption across institutions, and existing studies provide limited localized evidence on how specific digital channels influence financial performance. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to examine the effect of digital transformation in banking on the financial performance of commercial banks in Uasin Gishu County, Kenya. It specifically assessed the influence of mobile banking adoption, internet banking adoption, agency banking adoption and ATM adoption on financial performance measured through return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE) and net interest margin (NIM). The study was anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovation Theory, Resource-Based View and Transaction Cost Theory. The study adopted a longitudinal panel research design and targeted the 39 licensed commercial banks in Kenya. A purposive sample of 12 commercial banks with complete records was observed over the period 2018–2025, yielding 96 bank-year observations. Secondary data were obtained from Central Bank of Kenya reports, audited financial statements and annual bank reports using a structured data extraction sheet. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and panel regression analysis in STATA version 17.0, supported by diagnostic and model specification tests, and the random effects model was selected on the basis of the Hausman test. The findings revealed that the four digital banking channels jointly explained 78.0% of the variation in financial performance. Mobile banking adoption had the strongest positive and significant effect on financial performance, followed by internet banking adoption, agency banking adoption and ATM adoption, all of which had positive and significant effects. The study therefore recommends that commercial banks should enhance mobile banking platforms through improved usability, reliability and cybersecurity; strengthen and integrate internet banking systems; expand agency banking networks while improving agent support and service quality; and modernize ATM infrastructure and integrate it with other digital channels.

title: A novel smart partial least squares-based model for analyzing key factors driving green finance and accounting companies’ performance in big data era
summary: Sustainability in the business world, particularly in the financial sector, entails adopting strategies and practices that benefit both the environment and society, while also ensuring the profitability and financial growth of companies. This concept is becoming a critical factor in assessing green financial performance, as companies that adhere to sustainability principles can manage their resources more efficiently and are more resilient to environmental and economic changes. The analysis of large data sets through big data technologies enables companies to collect extensive environmental, social, and economic information, supporting more informed sustainable practice decisions. Green finance is a relatively new concept that offers an option for green financing to individuals, corporate entities, and governments that are willing to finance and invest in green activities or low-carbon initiatives. The use of big data in green finance facilitates a more accurate assessment of investment opportunities and risks associated with green and low-carbon projects. This paper proposes the Smart Partial Least Squares model to investigate the performance and growth determinants of green finance and accounting firms. As green practices gain traction in the financial industry, it becomes crucial to identify the factors that explain the success of green finance. The proposed model considers both technology-based changes and managerial perspectives in evaluating the key performance drivers. Big data technologies, such as machine learning and artificial intelligence, can be leveraged to gain a deeper understanding of the impact these drivers have on green finance and accounting firms. The results indicate that both internal factors (technological variables and management variables) and external factors (economic variables, legal and regulatory variables) significantly contribute to the growth and efficiency of green finance firms, providing valuable insights for practitioners and policymakers. The research results show that this interaction between internal and external factors is effective in creating a positive cycle between sustainability and green financial performance, which can lead to sustainable and long-term growth of companies in competitive markets. Managers should note that any improvement in ICT application may contribute meaningfully to the overall performance of green finance and accounting firms. This research will contribute to the literature on the performance of green finance and accounting companies by integrating all the mentioned variables, including the role of big data in optimising green finance strategies.

title: EFFECT OF CORPORATE GOVERNANCE ON THE FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF DEPOSIT MONEY BANKS IN NIGERIA
summary: This study examines the influence of corporate governance on the financial performance of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria between 2018 and 2024 using an ex-post facto research design. Data were sourced from the annual reports of fourteen (14) banks and the Central Bank of Nigeria’s Statistical Bulletin and analyzed within a panel framework. After a Hausman test favored fixed‐effects estimation, financial performance was operationalized via the return on assets (ROA), while governance variables included board meetings and board diversity with bank size as a control variable. The findings reveal that board meeting has significant positive effect on financial performance whereas board diversity revealed insignificant negative effect on financial performance. The study recommends that banks should institutionalize a structured meeting calendar that guarantees regular and substantive engagement on risk oversight. This can be facilitated by incorporating a practice of quarterly or more frequent meetings focused explicitly on capital adequacy, liquidity stress testing, and emerging risk trends, boards can convert meeting frequency into a strategic tool for early warning and corrective action. And also, banks should pursue efforts to build an inclusive culture and continuous learning environment that ensures the full advantages of gender diversity are tapped. This may be advanced through mentorship schemes which encourages the pairing of seasoned directors with new female appointees. This can help translate demographic diversity into deeper insights and more robust decision-making.

title: Green strategic orientations and enterprise performance in SMEs: The mediating role of green innovation
summary: This study examines how green strategic orientations contribute to enterprise performance (EP) in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) under increasing environmental and market pressures. Drawing on the natural resource-based view (NRBV) and recent evidence on green innovation (GI) and sustainable performance in SMEs (Liu et al., 2024), it distinguishes between green market orientation (GMO) and green learning orientation (GLO) and investigates their roles in driving GI. Using survey data from 415 Chinese manufacturing SMEs, structural equation modeling with bootstrap analysis is employed to test the proposed relationships. The results show that both GMO and GLO have significant positive effects on GI and EP. GI serves as a partial mediating mechanism linking strategic orientations to performance. Notably, GMO exerts a stronger influence on GI than GLO. These findings suggest that market-driven green strategies provide more immediate triggers for innovation, whereas learning-driven strategies support longer-term capability development. Overall, the results indicate that, under resource constraints, SMEs may achieve faster performance gains through externally oriented green strategies. The study provides practical insights for SME managers in prioritizing green strategic investments and aligning strategic orientation with innovation efforts to enhance performance, thereby contributing to the emerging literature on GLO and sustainable EP in SMEs (Rehman et al., 2024).

title: Developing an Asset Management Audit Framework and Effectiveness Index for Kazakhstan’s Quasi-Public Sector
summary: Effective asset management of quasi-public sector organizations is an important condition for improving economic efficiency, quality of corporate governance and sustainability of business processes. The purpose of this study is to develop a conceptual model of asset management audit adapted to the conditions of Kazakhstan and to propose an Asset Management Effectiveness Index (AMEI). The methodology includes a systematic review of the literature on the PRISMA protocol, a thematic analysis of selected studies, and an illustrative analysis of the activities of JSC NC KazMunayGas. Scientific publications for 2012-2020 and consolidated financial statements of KazMunayGas under IFRS for 2022-2023 were used as initial data. Based on the results of the thematic analysis, seven key areas were identified: independence of auditors, application of INTOSAI standards, asset management audit methodology, corporate governance and accountability, features of Kazakhstan’s quasi-public sector, audit quality control mechanisms, and financial benchmarking. On this basis, a five-stage audit and AMEI model is proposed, which includes five equally weighted components, evaluated on a scale from 0 to 10. KazMunayGas’s illustrative data shows that in 2022-2023, revenue decreased from $18,860 million to $18,236 million. The results show the practical significance of the proposed model for a comprehensive assessment of the asset management system; however, calculating and empirically validating AMEI require access to internal audit documentation and informed business decisions in quasi-public sector organizations.

title: Absolute Environmental Sustainability Assessment of an Avocado Oil Supply Chain
summary: The increasing demand for avocado oil raises the question of whether production and consumption remain within environmentally sustainable limits. This study evaluated a cradle-to-grave avocado oil supply chain, produced in Colombia and consumed in Germany, by integrating Life Cycle Assessment with planetary-boundary-derived environmental budgets. The production and consumption of 1 kg of avocado oil generated 7.13 kg CO2-eq, 0.0074 kg P-eq, 0.0068 kg N-eq, 0.1875 m2·a crop-eq, and 1.95 m3 world-eq deprived for climate change, freshwater eutrophication, marine eutrophication, land use, and water use, respectively. Monte Carlo analysis (1000 iterations) indicated that the LCIA results were relatively stable with respect to the inventory uncertainty represented in the background data. We compared the environmental impacts associated with a hypothetical annual intake scenario in which the EAT–Lancet recommended intake of unsaturated oils is supplied entirely by avocado oil with allocated Safe Operating Space budgets. Under equal per-capita sharing, the per-person environmental entitlement is identical across geographical perspectives; geographical differentiation arises only when region-specific sharing factors, such as the economic/FCE factor, are applied. The results show that sustainability conclusions depend strongly on the principle used to share the available environmental capacity among products and activities.

title: Islamic Law in the Age of Technology and Digital Economy: Reconstructing Epistemology, Addressing Regulatory Challenges, and Rethinking the Future of Contemporary Fiqh
summary: This study analyzes the transformation of Islamic law in digital ecosystems, identifies epistemological and regulatory challenges, and formulates an integrative framework for contemporary fiqh. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, blockchain, smart contracts, sharia-compliant fintech, and crypto-assets have transformed economic transactions while exposing limitations in conventional Islamic legal responses to digital phenomena. Using a Systematic literature review with qualitative thematic synthesis, the study examines scholarly publications, fatwas and legal decisions, regulatory documents, and supporting academic literature. The findings show four interconnected developments: digital transactions alter the manifestation of ownership, consent, contractual execution, and responsibility; classical uṣūl al-fiqh remains essential but requires contextual reconstruction through maqāṣid al-sharīʿah and technology-sensitive analysis; regulatory lag, cross-border transactions, digital-asset uncertainty, and AI ethics create significant governance challenges; and future Islamic legal governance requires multidisciplinary and adaptive institutional coordination. The study proposes the Neo-Digital Islamic Legal Framework (NDILF), integrating classical jurisprudential foundations, maqāṣid-oriented evaluation, digital ethics, and adaptive regulation through an iterative process of technological identification, multidisciplinary analysis, fatwa formulation, regulatory translation, and social-impact assessment.

title: Process–project model of management cost accounting in construction enterprises
summary: The article substantiates the organizational and methodological foundations of a process–project model of management cost accounting for construction enterprises aimed at overcoming the information gap between project costing, process-based resource consumption, and responsibility centres. Systems and process approaches, as well as methods of classification, comparison, grouping, and structural-logical modelling, are applied. A system of internal indicators is developed to ensure a consistent link between business transactions, consumed resources, business processes, construction projects, work stages, and responsibility centres. Rules for the direct attribution of costs and the causal allocation of indirect costs using appropriate cost drivers are substantiated. A “business process – construction project” matrix is proposed, enabling both the analysis of an individual project’s cost structure by process and the comparison of identical process costs across projects. An internal reporting format is developed to compare budgeted costs, flexible standards for actual output, and actual costs, while identifying the causes of variances, responsible persons, and corrective management actions. The scientific novelty lies in integrating project costing, process accounting, causal cost allocation, and responsibility control into a unified information model. The model is extended by incorporating environmental cost drivers and ESG indicators related to material circularity, resource reuse, waste management, and resource and energy efficiency. Its practical value lies in improving the accuracy of cost allocation, the timeliness of cost control, and the validity of management decisions, while providing an information basis for ESG reporting without establishing a parallel accounting system. title: From Microscope to Monitor: The Digital Transformation of Veterinary Pathology
summary: Pathology has traditionally been synonymous with the microscope, glass slides and the trained eye of the pathologist. However, advances in imaging technology, computing and artificial intelligence are transforming this conventional approach. Digital pathology involves converting glass microscope slides into high-resolution digital images that can be viewed, stored, analysed and shared electronically. In veterinary medicine, this technology has applications in diagnosis, telepathology, education, research, disease surveillance and quantitative image analysis. Whole-slide imaging allows an entire tissue section to be examined on a computer screen, while artificial intelligence and machine-learning tools are opening new possibilities for automated image analysis and computer-assisted diagnosis. At the same time, challenges related to infrastructure, cost, data storage, standardisation, validation and cybersecurity need to be addressed. Digital pathology is therefore not simply a replacement for the microscope; rather, it represents an evolution of pathology that can extend the reach and capabilities of veterinary pathologists.
